I selected "The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry" to read and review because I loved "Major Pettigrew's Last Stand," a book to which it was compared in the publisher's preview. And while I prefer "Major Pettigrew" for its pacing and multicultural appeal, I wholeheartedly recommend "Harold Fry." It has charms of its own.

Henry David Thoreau observed, "The mass of men live lives of quiet desperation," and I could not help but recall this quotation as I began Rachel Joyce's lovely debut novel. As the novel begins, Harold is merely existing. The reader is not given many details, but it is clear that Harold's marriage to Maureen is an empty shell, and that there are problems in his relationship with his adult son, David. Then Harold gets a farewell letter of sorts from a friend, Queenie Hennessy, and his carefully orchestrated charade of a life begins to come apart. Queenie had "done something nice" for Harold twenty years previous, and he always regretted not thanking her. Whatever this is is shrouded in mystery, and many readers will suspect a long-past affair. All these questions are a bit disconcerting, but if the reader is patient, all will be resolved.

Harold writes a "pro forma" response to Queenie's note, but as he goes out to mail it, something prevents him from putting it in the first mailbox he comes to. He passes postbox after postbox, and eventually makes an impulsive decision to walk from his hometown to Queenie's hospice, about 600 miles. Thus begins his transformation from a kind of living death to fullness of life.

Readers who are familiar with Joseph Campbell's "The Hero's Journey" will immediately recognize the motif: the hero leaves the world he knows to embark on a quest. Along the way he meets both helpers and tempters, and he eventually returns to the known world with a fullness of knowledge or with something to enrich his community and himself.

Harold Fry fits this motif to a tee. He meets many people and even animals along the way, and he gains something of value from each of them, even those who would deter him from his quest. Meanwhile, back at home, Maureen is undergoing her own transformation as she worries and responds to Harold's calls, postcards, and gifts. Nothing is as Harold or Maureen expect it to be. And the end of the quest is rewarding, but not in the way Harold imagines.

One final observation: This is a beautifully written novel. Most readers will love the use of language, especially in descriptions of the natural world. I am stunned that this is the author's first novel, though she has written many screenplays for the BBC. I hope to read much more of her work.

Most readers will like and appreciate "Harold Fry" if they persevere through the ambiguity at the beginning. Everything falls together eventually, I promise! Highly recommended.

Gretchen Moran Laskas's The Miner's Daughter is a haunting story of poverty set in a Depression-era mining town in West Virginia. Willa Lowell and her large, loving family are trapped in a mining ghost town with no chance for work, meaning no food other than meager rations of soup beans and thin cornbread. Willa's mother has just completed a difficult, dangerous pregnancy, and as the eldest daughter, Willa is responsible for household chores and for watching the other children while her mother recovers.

The other mining families are just as hard-hit by the Depression, especially those who are foreign-born like the Olivettis, immigrants from Italy. Willa is sensitive and intelligent, and loves to read, so when a missionary comes offering a large library of pristine books, Willa devours them in-between chores, beginning with classics such as Little Women and working her way into more difficult poetry by Poe and Whitman.

When Willa's father and half-brother Ves leave to search for work at Hawk's Nest, Willa is left to hold down the precarious fort. As her mother's too weak to work, and the next-oldest is only ten years old, Willa must masquerade as a boy in order to pick in the fields; otherwise, the family would starve. She meets Johnny Settle, a boy around her own age who is smitten by her intelligence and courage, and the two begin a bashful courtship.

The remainder of the novel chronicles Roosevelt's projects as part of the New Deal, including a personal visit to the Riley Mines by Mrs. Roosevelt that has a huge impact on the Lowells' lives. The author includes brief notes as to actual New Deal settlements created by the Roosevelts, as well as several websites that give further information about real places and events in the story.

Miner's Daughter is written with great sensitivity towards the harsh realities of poverty, including poignant contrasts between the haves and the have-nots in a nearby town. This is a book that is just as pertinent today in a time of recession, inflation, and rising unemployment, and a book that speaks volumes on the warmth and love of family and the need for all of us to realize our dreams.

The UPRIGHT SMART WEARABLE POSTURE TRAINER is an "anti-slouch" posture trainer that really works! I discarded my [[ASIN:B00N9P8GMW Lumo Lift]] after a week or so, because my sitting posture is pretty good, and I rarely slouched badly enough to trigger the Lumo Lift. In contrast, the Upright buzzes me whenever I start to relax my posture even partway to a full slouch.

The Upright needs to be pasted to your back with gentle adhesive pads (60 included), rather than pinned to your clothing (like the Lumo Lift), but the greater sensitivity makes the extra effort worthwhile. Packets of one-time-use adhesive pads are available from the Upright web site for about $15.

You can wear the Upright between your shoulder blades if you're going to be standing, walking, and sitting; or at the small of your back if you're an Upright novice or generally sitting. As long as it's turned on, the Upright works even without the accompanying app (Android or iOS) that tracks your training progress. The Upright app uses Bluetooth to connect with the wearable Upright.

The app walks you through the simple setup, which mostly involves (1) finding the proper spot for placement on your back, and (2) calibrating the device so that it can detect a slouch. Once it's calibrated, the device will gently buzz you whenever you sink into a slouch--which inevitably happens as your muscles tire from holding a single position--so that you can straighten up. (There is no sound. The product page video that demonstrates the buzz is kind of amusing.)

When you create an account (free), the app collects information about your height, weight, and age, and then generates a daily posture training program that is personalized for you. The training program begins with your wearing the device for a few minutes, and then for longer and longer sessions. At the end of a session, the app gives you a score, based on how long you held your upright posture. (Mine was only 86%, because I intentionally slouched to test the buzz.)

The Upright arrives fully charged. The app tells you how much charge is remaining in your Upright. When you're charging the device in the supplied charging dock, a solid red light tells you that it's properly connected and charging.

The City of Ember is falling apart. The Builders designed the city generations ago, but only provided for its survival for 200 years. The secrets to saving the city have been lost, and now the citizens are in a panic as their provisions run low and confusion sweeps through the masses.

Enter 12 year old friends and recent school graduates Lina and Doon. They are both convinced that answers are within their reach, and when Lina finds an old, mysterious document - chewed up and partially destroyed by her baby sister - the friends work together to fill in the missing pieces of the message. They are optimistic and courageous, and their perserverence has profound effects on the future of Ember.

There is an interesting paradox in the world DuPrau has created here - while it seems to take place in the future, the lives of the citizens are very primitive. There is no technology for communication and colors like green and blue only exist as expensive and rare colored pencils. The entire city is lit by a system of floodlights, the citizens being woken at 6am when the system turns on, and going to bed at the 9pm "lights out." No one has discovered how to make "moveable light," so they are absolutely restricted to the city's schedule. Knowledge is limited, and children only go to school until the age of 12. The city library is a mostly unused vault of makeshift books. The shadows beyond the city are called the Unknown Regions, and very few dare to enter them.

I like the small details that hint at life beyond Ember - mainly, Doon's fascination with bugs, and Lina's care of a tiny bean sprout. It's this curiosity in both of them that make them the most likely saviors of Ember. It seems that everyone else is content in their ignorance, an extension of the darkness that is always just a breath away. Darkness without, darkness within.

For me, the story just sprang to life in the last quarter of the book. I simply could not stop reading until I found out what was going to happen to Lina and Doon. I cared about them, I cared about Ember. I think part of DuPrau's success with this book is that she follows the "Show, Don't Tell" approach and let's us see through the characters' actions who they are and why we should care about them.

I've been careful not to give anything away in this review, but just know that there are several interesting revelations and an intriguing foundation for the continuation of this story, found in DuPrau's sequel, People of Sparks.

I have had varied experiences with Christian devotionals, some being good and on target while others pushed an agenda of some kind and were more of a diversion than a focus on God. I got a sense that this one was different than the typical devotional book and I was right, and it is different in good ways.

This is a short devotional book designed to be read over the course of a month. Each reading is about 2-3 pages in length and even a slow reader can get through one in 5-10 minutes. The writing is very approachable and relatable - so many devotionals read like heady sermons or research papers, and this one reads more like a letter from a friend.

I like the format and approach. Each reading is broken up into four sections: Spiritual Development, Prayer Starter, Change the Way You Think, and finally Challenge. The Spiritual Development section is the meat of each reading, starting with a block of Scripture and followed by a discussion on it. The Prayer Starter section is just what it sounds like - a starting point for prayer. The Change the Way You Think section could be renamed “Application” as it focuses attention on how to use the previous information from the first section. And Challenge provides an activity that executes application.

So, behind this whole devotional book is the idea that we all have creativity that can be mined and accessed, and for some the issue is focus or confidence instead of lack. The idea here is to spark creativity and draw it out, and each reading focuses on some aspect of creativity - starting with a Scriptural concept. It’s a different approach and it works. If you work through this book you will either find you have creativity you didn’t know you had or you will figure out how to access your creativity even when you’re in a “dry spell”.

This is a different kind of devotional. It is written for those who want to access their creative side while maintaining a Biblical perspective. It’s well-written, well organized and it definitely will get you thinking more creatively.

I am hoping they will release a kindle edition. This is a very thoughtful and academic appreciation of Virginia Woolf that I heartily recommend for the first or 15th time reader of Woolf.

Book Description: Behind this study of Virginia Woolf's novels is an intense interest in the person revealed in the novelist. The criticism is warm as well as acute and the whole study is felt to be a tribute reasoned and justified.

2nd edition (July 25, 1975) Back Matter: More than most novelists, Virginia Woolf benefits by an introducer. She is never, either by intention or equipment, the expected novelist. She chose the novel to adapt it deliberately and progressively to be the vehicle of her own subtle perception. Behind this study of the novels is an intense interest in the person revealed in the novelist. The criticism is warm as well as acute and the whole study is felt to be a tribute reasoned and justified - to a woman sensitive, compassionate, passionately honest and eager only for truth; to an artist quite unsparing of her own labour, finely gifted, self-effacing, serious and humourous. Bennett added two chapters on A Writer's Diary and on Virginia Woolf's critical essays for the second edition. Both can help our understanding of Virginia Woolf the novelist; the Diary by the insight it gives into her creative process and the fuller understanding we can gain of technical problems, the essays because they are about novels and novelists.

Review of the hardback: 'A critical study which strikes me as a real service to us all and to the fame of the author it expounds. ... The closest discussion of Virginia Woolf's methods as a novelist I have read and some of the most penetrating appreciations of her mind and style that have been written.' Desmond McCarthy, The Sunday Times

KIRKUS REVIEW: The novels of Virginia Woolf, her treatment of character, of narrative sequence, of moral values and of form -- and within these categories, her development from uncertain, experimental beginnings to maturity and genius as a writer. This critical appraisal of her work is intelligent, extensive, sympathetic, but the copious quotations from the author herself suggest that what one should learn of Virginia Woolf is to be found by reading her own books. This may serve as a guide in that direction. The market? The selected literary minority already enthusiastic admirers. Pub Date: Sept. 27th, 1945 ISBN: 052109951X

Joan Bennett (1896-1986), also known as Joan Frankau and born Aline Frankau, born in London, England, was a Cambridge literary scholar and critic. She was the daughter of Arthur Frankau (1849-1904) and writer Julia Frankau (1859-1916). She married Cambridge literary historian Henry Stanley Bennett (1889-1972) in 1920. She was educated at Wycombe Abbey School and in Hamburg and Paris and came to Girton to read Modern Languages then English, 1916-19. She was a University Lecturer in English 1936-63, a Fellow of Girton, and College Lecturer in English 1953-63 (Life Fellow 1963-86), and wrote one of the first critical studies of Virginia Woolf. In 1959, she was one of the expert witnesses for the defense in the Lady Chatterley Trial, she confirmed D.H. Lawrence's reputation as a novelist,

Publications by Joan Bennett include—
Four Metaphysical Poets – Donne, Herbert, Vaughan, Crashaw, Cambridge University Press 1934
George Eliot – Her Mind and her Art, Cambridge University Press 1948
Sir Thomas Browne – "A Man of Achievement in Literature", Cambridge University Press 1962
Five Metaphysical Poets – Donne, Herbert, Vaughan, Crashaw, Marvell, Cambridge University Press 1964

GOLD OF OUR FATHERS is the fourth "Darko Dawson" mystery (the first one that I've read), and it works fine as a standalone. Set in Ghana, the novel really brings this exotic (to U.S. readers) background to life, with its widespread poverty, corrugated-tin-roofed buildings, and police stations so underfunded that detectives must hire taxis to reach crime scenes. As one character notes: "This is Ghana. You do whatever you can to get money." Unfortunately, as a police procedural, the novel is a plodder, as it follows the likeable Chief Inspector Darko Dawson from place to place and interview to interview.

In the novel, Dawson is unexpectedly transferred, for one year, from the Criminal Investigations Division at Accra to the position of supervising Crime Officer at Obuasi, a backwater even by Ghanian standards. Upon his arrival, he finds that the police headquarters is a disorganized mess, and that its undisciplined officers seem to have forgotten the Ghanian Police Service motto ("To Protect and Serve with Honor").

On Dawson's second day, two "galamsey" gold miners discover the mine's Chinese owner buried in the gravel pit they are working. The owner was tied up, wrists to ankles, and buried alive. By the time Dawson reaches the scene (by hired taxi, fee negotiated), the body has been dug up, removed to a shack, and washed. Also, the crime scene has been thoroughly trampled by curious onlookers. Dawson's investigation is further complicated by language difficulties--knowing no Chinese, he must interview suspects and witnesses who speak neither English nor any Ghanian language.

Dawson also encounters hatred--by Ghanians for the immigrant Chinese who are destroying the Ghanian landscape with their illegal gold-mining operations; by the Chinese for the Ghanians that they see as "lazy black people wanting money for no work"; by the mine workers for their cheating bosses who make them wait for their daily pay. Naturally the highly competent detective Dawson finds a way to solve the crime despite all these obstacles.

GOLD OF OUR FATHERS is well-written, but in rather formal English. That, along with all the attention the author pays to describing the Ghanian locale, and the author's decision to sprinkle in authentic Ghanian words to add verisimilitude, makes for an extremely slow-moving mystery novel. (There is an excellent glossary of Ghanian words, with easy-to-understand definitions, in the back of the book; there is a map of Ghana and a helpful cast of characters in the front of the book.) The plot is complex and satisfying; but because the narrative just plods along, I rate this novel at a somewhat stingy 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

I have mixed feelings about this book that I have been reading and reviewing for the last 35+ days. On one hand it is five stars because it is chock full of wonderfully rich recipes, two of which I made (pictured - Tortilla Espanola ala Michelle and Pots de Creme). On the other hand it is also full of great recommendations for essential kitchen tools but which are more for the slightly advanced cooks.

I actually had to buy stuff, such as this [[ASIN:B0023PVZD6 Scanpan CTX 12-3/4-Inch Covered Chef's Pan]], [[ASIN:B072BRFK2N HERBS DE PROVENCE]], and several other items in order to make the recipes because they were not part of my kitchen arsenal and I have a tremendous amount of cooking tools.

The book starts out with which rolling pin is the best and moves on from there to recipes using a rolling pin and techniques on how to roll noodles, etc. She also provides cooking tips with some of the recipes, many of which I never heard of. For example, on troubleshooting slurry, you need a small amount of liquid with cornstarch whisked in instead of sprinkling it on which creates a lumpy slurry. Personally, I do not even know what slurry is and she does not explain it. It is apparently a semi-liquid mixture per my Internet search.

I do wish she defined things more so the novice cook would understand what is meant. For example, when I was making the Pots de Creme recipe, she says to simmer until "steam starts to wisp around the edges." I had to assume it was when bubbles formed around the edge because my boyfriend and I never saw any steam around the edges.

In summary, this is an absolutely fabulous book that is a great complement to a well-stocked cooking library. It is NOT for the novice cook but for one who is more seasoned or wants to become so. The recipes are stupendous and rich. My boyfriend was blown away by both of the ones I made. It has more recipes than tips, in my opinion. I also would have preferred pictures of some tools (like the spider she recommends; I did not even know what kitchen tool that was). In addition, a glossary of some terms would be great as well. Nevertheless, the only reason I rated this 4 stars is because the title of the book is not true to what is inside. It is more cookbook than anything and the tools are not for the home cook but are more for the more ADVANCED cook in my opinion. I also would expect a book with this title to start with utensils such as knives, forks, pots, and pans instead of rolling pins, sheet pans, cast iron, etc. in that order.

This book reminded me of the time I was a total pushover. I remember the specific moment of when that changed for me. When I was 17 years old, my high school classmates had all agreed to play hooky after the prom. I refused and attended school the next day. I was the only one in class. I was actually eager to learn on my own and have the teachers to myself, but they decided to cancel class. I was disappointed but I did not speak up. SHAME ON ME! Well at the end of the year, they gave out the yearly awards. I expected to receive the perfect attendance award as I had every year. However, the nun said that they were not giving out perfect attendance this year since everyone else had played hooky. Then she said, "I hope you don't mind." I just grunted "uh" and shrugged my shoulders as if that were okay. SHAME ON ME! Although I think perfect attendance awards are ridiculous, it was still not okay with me. From that point on I have stood up for myself. If that happened to me today, I would say, "Actually, I do mind very much! I did have perfect attendance. My classmates absence has nothing to do with my attendance. I have earned that award." Let's say I did say that. Even if I did not get the award after speaking up, at least my feelings would have been made known and I would not have been such a doormat.

Since then I live my life this way. I even told three different doctors on five occasions that they were wrong and guess what, I was eventually proven right. This book is all about that. Challenging what is wrong and right and sticking up for yourself.

TEACH YOURSELF VISUALLY SAMSUNG GALAXY S5 is a very thorough, complete guide for setting up and using the Samsung Galaxy S5 smartphone. Exact screenshots from the Galaxy S5 explain every button and every procedure, showing exactly what a user should be seeing on the phone at every moment, while following the simple, detailed, step-by-step written instructions. The screenshots are overlaid with lettered and numbered circles that help the user quickly shift back and forth between the written-out steps and the related buttons shown in the screenshots.

Because it goes into so very much detail, this guide is probably best for someone who is new to using smartphones. If you're switching from another smartphone and mainly want to know what the Galaxy S5 buttons do, where things are located, and how to go about doing things you've already been doing, you may prefer a guide that isn't so closely tied to exact screen shots and specific steps--a guide that gives more help with actually understanding the phone's capabilities (e.g., [[ASIN:0789753499 My Samsung Galaxy S5]]).

With this guide, the fastest way to learn how to do something is to skip the rather brief, inadequate Index, and to check the Table of Contents for the general area of interest. The TOC lists the chapters by general subject and by detailed subchapters that explain the steps for each covered operation. For example, Chapter 11, Using Maps and Other Built-in Apps, includes the following subchapters: Find Your Location; Get Directions; Display Different Layers in the Maps App; Rotate, Zoom, and Tilt the Map; Explore with the Street View; Share a Location; Explore the Clock App; Explore Other Apps.

Because this guide is aimed primarily at new smartphone users, and awkward to use as a reference guide once you've learned the basics about using a Samsung Galaxy S5, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I selected this title because I like ethnic foods, Mexican and Tex-Mex being among my favorites. Good authentic Mexican food is not always easy to find, frequently being replaced with Americanized versions or, worse, fast food versions that leave much to be desired. I was hopeful that this book would help me create authentic dishes in my own kitchen, and so far it has not disappointed me.

This book, and its author, are the real deal. There are no cheap substitutions in this book, no compromises to make a recipe easier for a lazy chef while sacrificing authenticity, and no make-at-home fast food garbage. This book is packed with real, honest recipes that are representative of true Mexican cuisine. If you’re looking for a book that doesn’t take shortcuts and make substitutions for the sake of convenience, this is it.

Be aware – some people do not like cilantro, which is a very common ingredient in Mexican cuisine. Many, many recipes in this book call for cilantro. Keep this in mind.

This book is packed with full-color pictures. Not every recipe has a picture attached, but those that do not are in the minority. This is a colorful book that has all manner of eye appeal and really takes into consideration the adage “you eat with your eyes first”.

Each recipe is carefully written out with step by step instructions and clear directions on what to do. Many also include notes that offer up possible substitutions when practical without sacrificing authenticity. Where the author has varied from tradition or commonplace preps, notes explaining the variation are present.

This is a really good book on Mexican cuisine that produces authentic and flavorful dishes. It is well written, it is full of full-color photographs and the author sticks close to authenticity as much as possible. If you’re looking for a cookbook that will enable you to produce true Mexican dishes in your kitchen, this is a good one.

I’ve had this SSD for a few days and I also have a 1TB 970 Evo Plus and 1TB 860 Evo and all of them are great! But they do have their drawbacks too.

This drive does really well with SMALL (under 15Gb) workloads. The speeds are right up there (~500MB/s R/W) with my 860 Evo until it gets to about ~14GB at which point it slows down drastically. This is fine for things like boot, games, apps, and most programs.

However, if you do heavy workloads like video editing, file transfers, etc,. where you are regularly moving large (15GB+) files around this is NOT the drive for you. If you are a “heavy” user I highly recommend the 860 Pro. It can keep up those high R/W speeds without slowing down after ~15GB. It will maintain full speed throughout the duration of whatever you are doing.

With that said this is a great drive for light/moderate workloads (gaming, web browsing, small work files, etc.,) and it is at a price that gives you excellent value and quality for your money.

I would’ve happily paid a couple dollars more for it and it wouldn’t have cost Samsung that much so they could’ve made a little bit of extra profit by adding it.

I still recommend this drive though and would buy it or the 860 Evo again if I needed more storage.

"Travel is confusing." Yes, it is--and readers who don't pay attention to the details of the characters' conversations won't be able to follow this time travel story. THE TOURIST is probably the best time travel novel that I've ever read. The story--told by two viewpoint characters (Spens and Prisoner/Adorna/En)--immerses you in the time travel experience and its paradoxes (to be avoided? or nonexistent?). The characters really engaged me, so that the unexpected ending, which opened up new questions regarding the fate of many characters, left me feeling deeply saddened.

---Plot description that follows includes some SPOILERS---

At the novel's beginning, a 24th-century high-security prisoner (Prisoner/Adorna/En) is temporarily released to help an Agency official (Reimann) recover some important returning time travelers. A "translation" glitch in their Transport dropped them in one of Earth's ruined cities--and the Prisoner is the only living person who knows anything about the area.

The story then shifts to the experiences of a Happiness travel rep (Spens), who is assigned to an early-21st-century Resort managed by Tri-Millenium, a cheap time-travel-tours operation. It is Spens' job to shepherd Tri-Millennium's 24th-century clients around the curious 21st-century shopping malls, airports, and national parks. But when one of Spens' tourists goes missing, Spens is tasked with finding her. He's helped by a couple of female travel reps (Li and Edda); by a tattooed "extemp" from the 24th who's opted to live permanently in the 21st (Ivan); and by a couple of native thugs.

At one point Spens meets Reimann, who warns him to forget about the client. But Spens' bosses order Spens to carry on with his search. As he forges on, it begins to dawn on him that the missing client is no ordinary tourist; and it begins to dawn on the reader that the missing client may have something to do with the mysterious Near Extinction Event--still to come at the end of the 21st century--that destroyed most of Earth's cities and population. The 24th century is still rebuilding after the NEE, and no one in that century knows what caused it, because only those who completely missed the NEE survived.

Ultimately, THE TOURIST is about the consequences of the possible time paradoxes caused by the missing client's overlapping visits at different years in her life to the same few days in the 21st century; and by Reimann's efforts to "correct an error". Spens and his friends are residing in the 21st century at a time 60 years ahead of the NEE, but suddenly the 21st century social structure begins to disintegrate around them in a way that is NOT reflected in the "known" history of the time (as it is "known" to 24th-century historians). Did Reimann change something that changed future events in the other character's personal time lines? Or do future events happen exactly as before, exposing the fact that the characters' "known" time lines (that Spens and his friends were taught to accept) were only a "Big Lie" perpetrated by the all-controlling 24th-century government (Geneva)?

---End of plot description---

What makes this time-travel novel so unusual, is that the time travelers don't just go back in time, change something, and return to a world that is different from the one they left. Instead, the time travelers are living through, and directly experiencing, the changes apparently caused by a time paradox, so that their own future time lines are changing dynamically. Unless, of course, the time travellers have been lied to by the government all along about the actual historical facts.

There are no clear answers to the time paradox/government conspiracy question, and this is a very complex, hard-to-describe novel. But it is entertaining not only for the time travel, but also for the picture it paints of our century as viewed by tourists and travel agents from the 24th century.

For those not in the know, my title is from "My Big Fat Greek Wedding," in which John Corbett plays Ian Miller, a vegetarian high school teacher. His fiancee Toula's Greek family doesn't understand the meat-free concept. Thankfully, Diane Kochilas, author of several definitive cookbooks on Greek cuisine, does.

Although your first impression of Greek food might be the flaming cheese appetizer saganaki or greasy lamb or chicken gyros, many Greek recipes were meatless, particularly those that coincided with the fasting required by the Greek Orthodox calendar (48 days before Easter, 40 days before Christmas, and lesser fasting periods throughout the year in which meat and animal products were not allowed). The Lenten dishes in particular, called Lathera ("oiled"), consist of hearty bean stews, stewed eggplants, and other braised dishes with loads of olive oil as flavoring agent.

In addition to a brief cultural and culinary history of the Greek Islands, Kochilas also provides primers on various varieties of Greek olives (kalamata, conservolia, halkidiki, megaritiki, thrubolea), cheeses (feta, teleme, sfela, batsos, touloumotiri, galotiri, kopanisti, kasseri, graviera, kefalotiri, etc.), and a section devoted to bread (after such luscious descriptions of Greek bread, the book is noticeably lacking in bread recipes; a sore oversight). Greek flavor combinations of lemon, dill, olive oil, eggs, oregano and garlic, tomatoes and cinnamon, and others are also discussed in the introduction.

The book is dominated by vegetable and grain dishes, including a simple variation on the ubiquitous Greek salad. The recipes open with meze, or Greek appetizers similar to tapas. Some of the more unusual offerings include eggplant puree with walnuts, potato-garlic dip with walnuts, harvest pumpkin-chestnut puree, and spicy lentil and wild rice salad.

Main dishes are usually a grain-veggie combo, including numerous recipes for orzo (a rice-shaped pasta), bulgur, rice pilafs, and polenta. Soups include potatoes stewed with kalamata olives, tomato and rice, and artichokes stewed with potatoes, tomatoes, and mint. There is an entire chapter devoted to stuffed vegetables, and another to savory pies and homemade phyllo dough, including spanakopita, savory pumpkin pie in a phyllo coil, and onion pie with raisins, dill, and nutmeg.

The final chapter covers egg dishes perfect for a light brunch, including a baked omelet with chestnuts and feta, asparagus frittata, and scrambled eggs with fresh tomato and parsley.

The recipes are clearly written, and each chapter offers the cook a background on traditional Greek cuisine and regional cooking.

The only downside is that it may be difficult to locate the myriad of Greek cheeses (and olives) that Kochilas lovingly describes, particularly if you live in a small town that's not close to a Greektown. Also, I generally stick to a very-low-fat diet with no added oils, so I scaled back on the 1/2 cup or more of olive oil called for, but that's more a matter of personal taste (I recently read where Greeks have the highest per capita consumption of olive oil at 26 *liters* a year!!).

Anyone doing software development in a Linux/UNIX environment has likely had to work with make files. Even in a Windows environment, the make facility is an underlying component for a number of development systems though this likely is hidden from the user. A carefully crafted make file can greatly reduce time and effort during the build process and can make a very complex system very easy to build, but make itself is a complex and often hard-to-understand utility. This book seeks to demystify the make facility.

Building an application is usually more involved than just compiling a source file or two and then calling the linker. It often involves bringing in libraries from other locations, building dependencies, setting up environment variables and any number of other tasks required to successful building of the final application. It can also mean building source files written in different languages into object files. Make can handle all of these scenarios and more.

Managing Projects with GNU Make walks the reader through the process of building more and more complex make files, starting with a simplistic example that builds a small application, then starts getting into more interesting topics like setting rules, establishing multiple target types and eventually transitioning into much more involved systems that build very intricate projects. It explains how to set up make for building Java apps, though I don’t think I have seen too many Java projects that rely on make (perhaps because this book is a bit older now and there are more modern facilities for such).

My only issue with this book is that it does not seem to have a very logical ordering on certain things. Material is presented in a manner that, for me, requires some jumping around through the book and makes the material a little more complicated than necessary. This is not to say this is a bad reference, but it would benefit from more logical ordering. This build is more of a reference, not as useful as a how-to.

This is the one book that really goes in depth on how to use make for building projects. It’s an absolute must-have if your project relies on make and is a good addition to the library.

Have you ever had one of those books that is just full of common-sense solutions to a problem, all collected together in one place? This is that kind of book, and the problem it addresses is weight loss. This is not a diet book at all, but it is a book that is full of suggestions on how to make small changes to your everyday lifestyle that will better your health and help you lose weight. Of course, this is not a one-size-fits-all type of thing so it will not be the solution for everyone, but it is likely going to be appropriate for most in one or more ways.

As I mentioned, this is a common-sense approach to weight loss. It’s not about implementing a new diet or setting up a rigorous exercise program. Instead, it’s about making small changes here and there that will improve your overall health. As an example, one of the things it suggests is drinking more water. While that should be inherently obvious, what is not obvious is how it affects your body and why it’s helpful for weight loss, and the author explains that. Then, there are multiple suggestions for how to introduce more water consumption into your lifestyle. There are many more suggestions like this too, such as getting more sleep, getting more exercise, and eating more fruits and vegetables. All of that is common sense, and having it all together is good, but what makes this book work is that it suggests not just what, but why and how.

This is a fine book on weight loss for those that don’t want to deal with diets, exercise programs and all the trending weight loss ideas out there. This is a common-sense approach for small lifestyle changes with big dividends.

Because I love baseball, I really enjoyed reading this unusual mystery/thriller, THE SETUP MAN. Amateur private investigator Johnny Adcock is a 35-year-old, left-handed relief pitcher in the big leagues. He took his father's advice to look into relief pitching as a way to make easy money, and now earns $1.5 million a year by throwing a baseball for about two hours a week. He's the San Jose Bay Dogs' setup man--the guy who comes in during the eighth inning to pitch to just one left-handed batter.

With a job like that, Johnny has lots of free time, so he "moonlights" as a private investigator to relieve boredom. Professional baseball people approach him with their personal problems (cheating wives and girlfriends, crooked agents, whatever), and Johnny gets the dirt needed to resolve their situations. In this book, Johnny sets out to investigate a catcher's "wife problem". But when the catcher drives off a cliff--with a prostitute in his car's passenger seat--Johnny finds himself nearly in over his head. Not only does the investigation become a murder investigation, Johnny gets personally involved with two cold-blooded murders, gets seriously entangled with a pornography and prostitution operation that's growing exponentially by exploiting professional baseball players and other athletes, and nearly gets himself killed.

Because Johnny investigates between pitching assignments, there's a lot of good baseball background included in this novel. But Johnny explains the more esoteric baseball points as he goes along--seamlessly without intruding on, or interrupting, the narrative--so the reader needn't be a student of baseball to understand and enjoy this story.

THE SETUP MAN is well-plotted, with a complicated storyline but a believable ending. Because author T.T. Monday is a talented writer and storyteller who really understands baseball, I'm looking forward very much to reading his next baseball mystery. I hope that the next one will also feature the lazy, likeable, and memorable Johnny Adcock.

365 COMFORT FOODS is an excellent collection of standard American cooking recipes. So far, I've prepared two recipes from the "Comfort Food Classics Made Healthy" chapter ("Our Best Meat Loaf" and "Baked Eggplant Parmesan"), and two from the "Main Dish Meats, Poultry, and Seafood" chapter ("Pork Pot Roast in Cider" and "Swiss Steak"). All four dishes came out well, but the eggplant parmesan was a real star.

"Baked Eggplant Parmesan" is a recipe that tastes like classic eggplant parmesan, but skips the highly caloric step of frying breaded eggplant slices in olive oil. Instead, the eggplant slices are sprinkled with oil, coated with breading mixture, oven-baked on a sheet, and finished with tomato-cheese topping added for the last 8-10 minutes of baking. Delicious!

"Our Best Meat Loaf" produced a good, standard meat loaf that will not replace our family favorite meat loaf (our secret recipe uses carrots). However, the "Our Best" recipe will go into our meat loaf "rotation"--we make three different meat loafs, so we won't tire of the carroty one. "Swiss Steak" is one of the best recipes I've come across for beef cubed steak. The browned meat is simmered on the stovetop for 1-1/2 hours (or baked in the oven) in a sauce made from celery, carrots, onions, and a can of basil-garlic-oregano-seasoned tomatoes. "Pork Pot Roast in Cider", which I prepared in a slow cooker, resulted in a delicately-apple-flavored pork sirloin dish.

Like many housekeeping magazine editors' cookbooks, 365 COMFORT FOODS has recipes with longish lists of ingredients. For example, "Swiss Steak" calls for all-purpose flour, Hungarian paprika, salt, black pepper, cubed steaks, vegetable oil, specially seasoned canned tomatoes, celery, carrots, onion, water, and prepared mashed potatoes. Although Hungarian paprika and seasoned canned tomatoes are not exotic ingredients, they are unlikely to be found in every cook's pantry. Consequently, use of this cookbook requires some menu planning and special grocery shopping. In addition, most of the recipes (except for those in the "30 Minute Meals" chapter) require a fair amount of advance preparation time.

365 COMFORT FOODS is not a replacement for a good general cookbook like [[ASIN:0470560800 Better Homes and Gardens New Cook Book]], but it's a very good supplement to such a cookbook. You can never really have too many recipes for standard American "comfort" dishes! I'll definitely be fixing more of these recipes in the future, and I'm delighted to have finally found a tasty, healthful version of eggplant parmesan.

I selected this because my work computer runs hot and this fan is supposed to cool down a laptop by attaching it to the vent. I tried this on a Dell Latitude E6430 and the LED temperature reading climbs and my laptop heats up when connected. In fact, there's nothing about this product that would make me recommend it. Read on to see what is provided and what about this product is so wrong.

WHAT COMES IN THE PACKAGE:
- 1 laptop cooler fan
- 1 USB cable
- 1 plastic connector plate
- 4 rubber sticky feet and 3 (not 4 as specified) tiny silicone suction cups
- 1 instruction sheet
- 4 silicon mouthpieces to connect the fan to the laptop vent

WHAT IS WRONG WITH THIS PRODUCT:

- The instructions (picture attached) are incredibly poor and barely make any sense at all. Here are three sentences that I copied below exactly as written including punctuation and wording (except for the quotes I put around those sentences to indicate they were verbatim).

"Products with a bottom bracket accessories, and comes with three super sucker."
"Qingtai outlet end notebook, the silicone radiator outlet to trap the notebooks vents guide."
"According to the books of the heat, free adjustment"

- Assembly is slightly required and I had to figure it out on my own because the instructions were so poor.

* To assemble, I took the plastic black connector plate and snapped that into the three holes on the bottom front of the unit; the side closest to the on / off knob.

* I inserted the suction cups into the three holes in the front of the plate with the suction cups side down. Perhaps I could have used the rubber sticky feet but I'm not sure where to put those. I think the installation of those cushions is optional and I suspect they go either on the bottom of the connector plate or the unit.

* I attached one of the four silicone "mouth guards" to the front of the unit. I was sure to use the one that best fit the shape of the laptop vent so that it created a tight seal. Once assembled, I plugged one end of the USB cable into the side of the unit and the other end to a free USB port on my laptop.

* After the USB was connected, the temperature is displayed without ever having to turn on the unit or connect it to a laptop. I noted that the temperature without connecting the fan to my vent and with the fan off read 26.0 C. The LED is only in Celsius so I had to convert the numbers to Fahrenheit because I am not fluent in Celsius. I do know that the temperature is supposed to go down and not up so I turned on the fan but still did not connect the fan to my vent and the temperature started decreasing to 24.0 C and lower. However, once I connected the fan to the vent the temperature steadily increased to 31, 33, 36, 36.5 C, etc. I repeated all these steps on six separate occasions and got the same results. In exasperation, I decided to turn the unit around by facing the back of the unit toward the laptop vent. Once I did this, the temperature decreased slightly. This means that the fan is rotating the wrong way making this device useless.

In summary, this fan heats up the laptop. I suspect the reason for this is because the fan is rotating the wrong way so it is not drawing the heat away from the laptop vent. The temperature LED is only in Celsius which is great for Europeans fluent in that temperature but is not great for the majority of Americans. Also, the instructions are horrendous. My recommendation is to pass on this one.

UPDATE Jan 24, 2017 - I tried to see if I could fix this fan but could not. There are three tiny screws holding the body together. One screw is located underneath one of the rubber feet. Once I got it open, I had no way of knowing if the connectors are correct or not. The ribbons inside only go one way and reversing the fan doesn't seem to be an option. Therefore, I decided to throw the unit out since Vine reviewers have no warranty on the products they receive. What a waste.

I'm fairly new to gluten-free (GF) cooking and baking, although I've checked out several GF cookbooks from the library the last couple of years. I recently entered the world of GF baking with [[ASIN:1615190864 Nosh on This: Gluten-Free Baking from a Jewish-American Kitchen]], which served as an excellent primer for why GF flours and doughs react differently than their gluten-containing counterparts. I also learned how to create my own GF all-purpose mix using the recommended [[ASIN:B000216O16 Authentic Foods Superfine White Rice Flour - 3lb]] and [[ASIN:B00021639Y Authentic Foods Gluten Free Brown Rice Flour Superfine -- 3 lbs]]; I was surprised to see that Authentic Foods was not one of the reviewed/featured flour brands in the America's Test Kitchen book as they have received many excellent reviews from GF bakers. Naturally, I jumped at the chance of reviewing the "How Can It Be Gluten-Free Cookbook" as I am a fan of America's Test Kitchen and was looking for ideas for more gluten-free vegetarian dishes ([[ASIN:1557885109 The Gluten-Free Vegetarian Kitchen: Delicious and Nutritious Wheat-Free, Gluten-Free Dishes]] is also a great book).

The book starts off with brief overviews of the science of gluten, strategies for replacing wheat flour, a handy baking troubleshooting guide, choosing (or making) a GF all-purpose blend, a taste test of commercial GF flour blends, ATK's recipe for their all-purpose blend (unlike "Nosh on This," ATK uses the addition of nonfat milk powder to aid in browning, along with potato and tapioca starch), how to measure GF flours (they recommend weighing rather than volume), the use of binders, substitutions, and the gluten-free pantry, including reviews of commercial GF sandwich bread (seven of the eight received "recommended with reservations" or "not recommended") and gluten-free pastas; not surprisingly, the corn spaghetti and pasta scored the lowest. I liked their tip that rice noodles should NOT be cooked according to package instructions as they will fall apart; instead, it is recommended to soak them under very hot tap water for 20-45 minutes depending on the type of noodle. And be careful when purchasing soba, as not all soba is 100% buckwheat but may contain a mix of flours (I use [[ASIN:B005P0WMJ2 Eden Foods - Buckwheat Soba Pasta - 8 oz.]]). I also appreciated the in-depth guide (with photos) on the various types of whole grains, including rice as well as buckwheat, oat groats, millet and quinoa. Several methods are given for cooking grains: the pasta method, absorption method, and pilaf method. A chart explains which cooking methods are suited to which grains.

Beginning with breakfast, you'll find fluffy GF pancakes, waffles, crepes, quick breads, muffins, and coffee cake. I loved their quick method for steel-cut oats; because of the long cooking time, I never make them on weekdays, but here you boil the water, add the oats and let sit overnight. The next morning, you add additional liquid (milk, water, or juice depending on the variation) and reheat for 5-6 minutes. I tried several of the grain salads, including the wild rice pilaf with pecans and cranberries and the oat berry pilaf with walnuts and gorgonzola. I really enjoyed the blend of flavors and textures, especially the oat berry pilaf. I want to try the quinoa patties with spinach and sun-dried tomatoes at a later date as those also look promising.

Huge bonus points for including a chapter on making fresh GF pasta; this is the first GF cookbook I've seen that actually walks you through the steps, run the dough through your pasta machine and cut/shape your dough. I wasn't as impressed with the small variety of pasta sauces to go with commercial GF pasta (ATK's top pick was Jovial Brand) and would recommend [[ASIN:0936184582 Italian Classics (Best Recipe)]] instead. I loved the Asian-inspired noodle dishes like soba noodles with roasted eggplant and spicy basil noodles with crispy tofu.

The breads chapter makes the curious omission of not mentioning that gluten-free bread pans do exist; King Arthur Flour sells one made by USA Pan that is essentially a [[ASIN:B001TO3CN8 USA Pans 9 x 4 x 4 Inch Pullman, Aluminized Steel with Americoat]] minus lid. Gluten-free loaves need more support while baking, so a tall, narrow pan is better suited to this than a traditional loaf pan. Instead, ATK recommends the fussy process of making a foil collar similar to a souffle. I was pleased to see more international influences in the form of Soca (chickpea crepes from Southern France), arepas, pupusas, and pao de queijo.

The desserts chapters deserve special mention for their inclusion of elegant tarts (Nutella, Lemon, Rustic Walnut), gratins, pavlovas, and cakes. At the very back is a conversions and equivalencies chart and a weight-to-volume equivalencies for GF flours.

Overall, "How Can It Be Gluten-Free" sticks to ATK's standard format of lavishly illustrated product reviews, an ample description of why a given recipe works (and the food science behind it), and several variations for most dishes. I did find that there were far fewer bakeware recommendations (like the curious omission of the gluten-free loaf pan, or their take on whether silicone bakeware would work well for GF muffins, etc.). Each baked good comes with a handy chart with substitution instructions for commercial GF blends by Bob's Red Mill GF All-Purpose Blend and King Arthur Gluten-Free Multi-Purpose Flour, which is very handy if that's all you have on hand and time is short. There are plenty of variations (and international influences) to keep you happily experimenting for weeks (or months) to come. This is certainly a book I will find myself using on a regular basis, particularly for the many great meatless options, and a worthy addition to your gluten-free kitchen.

I needed a second battery for my Fuji X-T3 and I really wasn't excited by the price of the NP-W126S battery, so I looked for third-party replacements. After scraping user forums online and doing some additional research I settled on this one from Nitecore. It has proven to be every bit as good as Fuji brand batteries, and in some ways it's a little better.

I knew Nitecore as a manufacturer of flashlights and other light sources in particular. I was previously unaware of their batteries, so I was pleasantly surprised to discover that they had a battery that was an exact fit for my camera. It does fit perfectly, too - pops in and out without fuss and fits the charger without issue.

One of the issues with third-party batteries is that the camera will sometimes complain about it and throw up a message about a non-standard battery. I was initially concerned that this one would give me that issue but it has not - my camera accepts it without complaint and it just works.

I have been working with it for several months now, and it seems to actually last longer than the original battery that came with my camera (an actual NP-W126S battery). I have fully charged it one time, and since then I have taken well over 200 pictures with my camera (probably closer to 450) and it still has roughly 80% of the charge which is a big improvement. The thing that seems to drain my Fuji battery fastest is powering the camera on and off; this Nitecore battery seems to handle those cycles better.

It has overcharge protection and it stops charging when it reaches full capacity, even on the Fuji charger. I was concerned about using it on the original charger and considered getting the Nitecore charger to go with this battery, but it's perfectly happy on the Fuji charger.

I like the harder shell on this battery as compared to the original Fuji battery, Eventually this battery will fail; when it does, I am optimistic that the hard shell will keep it from swelling quickly so I can get it out of the camera when it finally starts to fail.

I am very happy with this replacement battery and based on my experience with it I can heartily recommend it. The camera doesn't complain about it, it has some built-in overcharge protection and it has a longer duty cycle than the original NP-W126S that came with my camera. When this one eventually fails, I'll get another one.

There seems to be a never-ending stream of study Bibles and devotional Bibles being brought to the market which makes selecting one all the more difficult. Do you select a good, solid study Bible that does a verse-by-verse analysis of scripture? Do you select a nice devotional Bible that has a very specific theme and has corresponding study helps included? Or what about a plain reading Bible, without any added material? And, how do you choose once you've narrowed down the field to the type of Bible you want? (And that does not even get into the foggy weather of deciding on a translation.)

If you want a devotional Bible, then the Life Journey Bible may be just the Bible for you.

The Life Journey Bible, based on the NIV translation, has devotional materials by Dr. Henry Cloud and Dr. John Townsend. The thematic idea behind the Life Journey Bible is growth and relationships - an area of human study about which Dr. Cloud and Dr. Townsend are well-versed experts. Their insights appear in several forms in this Bible, specifically in the sections marked "Insight" (devotional sections) and "Profile" (superb mini-studies in character for various Biblical figures), excellent essays on a variety of topics (including one regarding why some find it difficulty to share their faith with others) and finally chapter introductions that emphasize "growth lessons".

The Insight sections are brief, bite-sized nuggets of wisdom. Each is roughly one third of a page (half if you include the graphic that makes it stand out) and expands on a character lesson from the surrounding scripture passages. For example, the Insight titled "Improved Situations and Unimproved Character" focuses on Proverbs 30:21-23 and is located on the page facing those verses. This placement holds for all of the Insight sections. Matching devotional material with the verses to which they refer is something that I have seen done wrong in other devotional Bibles, so seeing it done right in the Life Journey Bible is a very good thing.

The Profile sections are one-page expositions on various characters in the Bible. These character write-ups offer some insightful information regarding character qualities including faith, forgiveness and obedience. As the Insight sections above, the Profile sections are in close proximity to the Scripture verses where one can find the character in question.

The essays are different in that they are two pages and are not focused on a single passage of Scripure but instead rely on multiple references scattered through the Bible. These essays again focus on character traits and show the reader some deep insights about feelings, relationships and service (among other topics). So far every one I have read has been very much on the mark and very Biblically based, and they seem to actually fit and belong.

Chapter introductions are not uncommon in Bibles of this type. That said, the Life Journey Bible chapter intros are different than others I have seen. In most Bibles that have such, the material often states that a book is written to the church at a specific place to address a specific situation, or a book is a handbook on Christian behavior, or even a book is a simple historical account. Instead, the Life Journey Bible explains chapters in terms of how they can help us grow, relate to one another and how to view ourselves.

In addition to the Scripture (the most important part, of course) and the added devotional materials, this Bible includes some useful study helps in the back. These include a table of weights and measures, some very nice reading plans, a subject index that alphabetizes the devotional material and lists pages where to find it all and finally a "Where to Find It" index for tracking down subjects of interest such as Leadership, Worry and Attitude. There are no maps in this Bible, though, which is a mild disappointment but certainly not a deal-breaker - maps aren't the focus.

The content of the material is all well and good but if the layout and format aren't good then the Bible loses appeal. Fortunately, this Bible is laid out nicely. The typeface is a little on the small side but is not so small as to cause eye strain. There is no redline. Section headings are set in a larger blue-grey sans font that is very easy to read and makes quick scanning easier (it would have been nice if the whole Bible were set in this font). The special sections are all bluish-grey in scheme and are aesthetically pleasing, flowing nicely without jumping off the page. All of the vibrancy is on the cover and dust jacket, actually - an eye-catching mustard yellow.

Finally, I should say something here regarding translation. To be perfectly honest, I am not a huge fan of the NIV and prefer the ESV instead (this is based on personal preference, not theological disagreement). The NIV is a fine translation, though, and it is geared toward the widest possible audience with its clear and straightforward wording. Basing this devotional Bible on the NIV is probably the best choice.

I have looked at several devotional and special-purpose Bibles that have had the feel of being poorly thought out and quickly rushed to market. The Life Journey Bible is not among those - this is probably one of the most well-planned and well-executed devotional Bibles I have been blessed to use. If I were to select a single devotional Bible for personal growth and understanding, this would absolutely be the one I would choose.

"Mister Death's Blue-eyed Girls" by Mary Downing Hahn is the somewhat-fictionalized story of a true event, the murder of two teen-aged girls on the last day of school in 1956. In an afterword, the author tells of her distant relationship with these girls and the impact their deaths had on her, her friends, and the entire community. She says that she has been trying to write this book for fifty years, and in my opinion, the resulting novel was well worth the wait.

The story is told from the points of view of various narrators, the main one being Nora, alter-ego of the author. Other narrators include Nora's best friend, Ellie; the boyfriend of one of the victims, Buddy; the murderer himself, Mister Death; and Mister Death's younger brother. There are also diary entries of several of the teenagers, which serve to fill in important background details. This multiple narrator device is useful for a crime novel in which only the murderer knows "who done it"; the terror and confusion experienced by the victims' friends result from the killer never being identified.

The novel is set in the fifties in Edgewood, Maryland, a suburb of Baltimore. The cultural references are perfect: the music, the clothing, the hairstyles, the drinking and smoking in the park, the pre-Vatican II atmosphere in the Catholic Church, the suffocating small-town ambiance, the rigid class divisions among the townspeople and the teenagers as well--all pitch perfect. The murders happen on the last day of school, and they abruptly force Nora and Ellie to realize that bad things can happen to your friends, not just to people on the news that you don't know. One major result of the crime is a crisis of faith in Nora. As she tries to understand how God could let such a thing happen to innocent girls, she is offered only platitudes by the priests of her church. She decides that she cannot believe in a God who can stand by and allow evil to happen.

At the same time, she is exploring her own literary interests, and this adds an important dimension to the book. She begins to read real literature, not the True Confession magazines she passed time reading before the tragedy. Poetry by Wordsworth, Walt Whitman, and T. S. Eliot; French novels, and modern American classics are all referenced, and they reinforce Nora's growing conclusion that the God she was taught about in church does not exist; that when we die, we become part of the earth forever. At one point, she describes herself as a pantheist. I found this part of the book very affecting; most people go through a crisis of faith at one point or another, and this one is well handled.

One other aspect of the book that will resonate with readers is the reaction of the townspeople to the murders and their desire to find and punish the killer. When Buddy is arrested, he is manhandled by the police, who release him after 48 hours because there is no evidence that he committed the crime. But none (or almost none) of the townspeople let a lack of evidence stand in the way of their judgment: they "know" that he did it, no matter what the police say. Buddy's life is made a living hell, and only Nora and one other minor character take his part. Of course, there are no Miranda warnings, and the rush to judgment prevents the police from finding the true killer. Readers may recall Columbine or other school-related shooting of recent years. This aspect is a good cautionary tale about how wrong we can be, even when we are sure we are right.

I give this book my highest recommendation. It is aimed at a teen audience, but I think adults will appreciate it as well, especially those of us who recall the fifties and are happy we have moved on as a society in so many ways. Readers will like Nora, an imperfect but appealing heroine, as she struggles with the unthinkable. Five stars.

I selected this book with the idea of expanding my library of available air fryer recipes. Being born and raised in the south I love southern cuisine, so this was a natural fit for me. It's a good book with some great ideas in it, but there are a couple of things about it that disappoint me.

This book is stuffed with southern dishes that have been adapted to the air fryer, and for that it is very successful. You can find recipes for grits, hush puppies, chicken fried steak and more, all of which are very much at the heart of southern cuisine. The recipes have been adapted to work in an air fryer instead of traditional deep fat or a skillet with bacon grease, making them healthier (in theory).

There aren't a lot of pictures in this book and that is a minor issue. It has been said many times that you eat first with your eyes, and that is true. Without pictures, it is more difficult to imagine a finished dish.

My main complaint is that there is no guide per recipe on the size of the air fryer that's needed. There are a couple of recipes in this book for pies, and they call for a 9" pie crust. I have two air fryers (a 3.5 qt. and a 6.5 qt.) and a 9" pie plate will not fit in either of them. Other recipes are similarly not suitable for smaller air fryers but will work in larger models. It would be nice to know what size air fryer is needed for a recipe like that.

In spite of the lack of pictures and no guide for what size air fryer to use, this is a good book with a great variety of air fryer recipes. If you like southern cuisine and want to make healthier versions of some of the classic dishes as well as new favorites too, this is a worthwhile book to check out.

Many cars on the market come with a rear-view camera that allows for seeing where the vehicle is moving when in reverse. Often the view appears on a dashboard screen. This is handy when parking and maneuvering while the vehicle is backing up. For vehicles that do not have a rear-view camera the alternative is to add on a kit that provides the same functionality. This is my first experience with such a kit and so far I am pleased with it. It does require doing a little work on the vehicle to set it up but the effort is worth it.

The package contains everything needed to set up this camera system. In addition to the camera and the screen, the kit includes the mounting screws for the actual camera as well as all of the wiring to connect everything together and to the power (reverse lights). There is also a mini-remote for interacting with the video screen though this is slightly inconvenient.

I spent a good deal of time reading and rereading the directions and concluded that the instructions could have been better. There are three pieces of documentation in the box; one shows a generalized set of four different configurations for connecting everything together (the fourth diagram on this sheet matches the configuration you want), one is a photocopied image of a wired system and the third is a “User’s Manual” which is one half-sheet of paper with a brief summarization of the product. There really needs to be a better documentation set than this.

If you are not skilled in working with electrical systems, either plan on this taking a good while or have someone you trust install the system. It’s not especially hard to set one of these up, but it does take some patience and a little bit of knowledge of the layout of the car’s wiring. I have worked on car electrical systems in the distant past so I had a vague familiarity, but it still took me a while to have everything set up and working.

Once wired the system is fairly straightforward to use. If it is wired up properly (meaning everything is connected to power on both ends and the two main components can see one another) it works nicely. The image when the camera is feeding to the monitor is bright and reasonably clear; the brightness can be adjusted as needed which helps when using this system at night. Another reviewer commented that he used a different camera connected to this system - while I am personally satisfied with the image quality, it’s reassuring to know that you can use another video camera if desired or necessary.

The addition of the remote will appeal to some, but for me it’s a component that can easily be lost. The menu system on the monitor provides the same functionality as the remote and this is good enough for me.

This is my first experience with rear-view video systems and though it gave me a little trouble setting up it was from lack of good documentation and inexperience, not from being a bad product. Once installed this is a nice and easy-to-use video system. Time will tell how long it works.

I normally think of storage media and batteries when I think of Maxell. That said, this is my second pair of Maxell headphones. My first pair is an ANC set that isn’t perfect, but they’re far and away better than I would ever have expected. These phones are not ANC phones, they’re just wireless listening phones. I was hopeful that they would be as good as my ANC phones in terms of sound quality, and Maxell has not disappointed me. They’re not perfect but they’re better than you can reasonably expect from the asking price.

Up front, let me say that I am not a big fan of on-ear headphones, and these fall into that category. I prefer an over-the-ear phone which to me is more comfortable. These aren’t bad for on-ear phones. This comes down to preference. If you are cool with on-ear phones, these will work for you, but if you have to have over-ear phones then you should consider other options.

The pads are soft enough, though they aren’t super cushy like some others I have used.

Being Bluetooth phones I immediately connected them to my phone. The connection went off without a hitch, though the phone was slower to find these than I had hoped. Once connected, they have been stable and reconnecting is much faster.

The real test is the sound profile. On my ANC phones, Maxell worked a miracle and got the sound profile nearly perfect even when the noise canceling is turned on. With these phones, the sound profile is not precise but it’s very balanced and better than average. The bass is strong but not throbbing like most headphones made these days. I like bass, but I don’t appreciate the insistence on pumping it so heavily that it gives me a headache. The midrange is full and music sounds like it has some depth without sounding like it’s playing from the bottom of a well. The highs are bright and clear, though on specific frequency ranges there is the slightest hint of distortion if you really look for it (and since I’m reviewing these, I went looking for it).

I cranked up the music as high as I could, and there was only a hint of distortion in the highs. And I had a headache when I was done.

Build-wise, these are not too bad. I would not pack them in a gym bag or anything like that, but these should work fine for a long while as long as they’re cared for properly. There’s enough flex in them to make them durable enough to survive some rough handling, but at the end of the day they’re primarily plastic - a drop from the right height or being crushed in a book bag will break them.

These phones are under $50 as I write this. What’s really distressing is that I have phones that are north of $200 that do not sound as good as these. Maxell knows how to make a good headphone that competes well with more expensive phones - I have two very different pairs to prove it. It begs the question - why are they only making budget headphones?

I would rate these slightly lower if the asking price were above the $50 mark. But, at the asking price you’d be hard-pressed to find headphones that sound better.

I have been baking homemade breads for my family for over 20 years and I have amassed a reasonable collection of books on breads, including some on sourdough breads. I was eager to see if this would be a good book for beginners as advertised. I have mixed feelings on it, though I can't call it a bad book.

The authors immediately launch into an explanation of how to build a basic starter cultuer in 6 days, and they explain in detail how to care for the starter, how to maintain it, and most importantly how to use it. All of this is fine information that a beginner needs.

Following that is a series of chapters filled with formulas for breads. There are chapters for artisan loaves, loaves made in pans, pizza and pastry recipes, and finally a chapter on dealing with leftover starter (with such things as waffles and other small breads). The formulas are all good introductory recipes for those just learning the art of working with sourdough.

So, my one criticism is actually on a subtlety of this book that I have not seen others mention. The formulas are all given in terms of mass, not volume. Typically, this is a good thing as it all but guarantees accurate and consistent results, and in itself this is the right way to make breads of most types. But, will a beginner want to deal with weighing out everything, including salt and water? Most beginners likely will not.

Adding approximate volume measures would have made this more approachable for the average beginner, though this assumes that by "beginner" we mean someone new to bread making in general.

If considering the thought that the target audience is experienced as a bread baker but new to sourdough baking in particular, this is not a bad book at all and is actually the right approach. However, if the reader is a rank beginner at bread baking in general, this might be a bit more overwhelming. It comes down to the definition of "beginner".

To me this WFPB (whole food plant based) diet is a lightly processed vegan diet without oil, salt, or sugar. Although it says sugar is not allowed, there are many recipes that call for maple syrup (like half a cup). I personally would not make a steady diet of recipes with maple syrup in them because that is sugar. There are about 100 grams of sugar in half a cup of maple syrup.

Now I have other vegan cookbooks that I would cook from. However, this book only has eight recipes I would ever consider making. 

I made the lime mint soup and put that over brown rice (see before and after photos). I did substitute chicken for vegetable broth because I am not only a plant-based eater and I have no interest in eating vegetable broth which tends to be very bland. The soup was okay over the rice but was still a little bit bland. The flavor of the lime sort of overpowered the dish. I wound up draining out all the liquids and only eating the solids over the rice due to the overpowering flavor. Mint and lime just does not go together for me.

There is an introduction and basics section up front before the recipes. I like the section on how to "cook the basics" such as rice, quinoa, potato, etc. However, I was surprised the steam cooking method was not even mentiond here.  I also like the "instead of this, eat that" section.

I am unsure yet whether this book will remain in my library. It probably will not get much use simply because most of the recipes I would not make and those that I would make have to be doctored up for flavor. Nevertheless, if one is interested in a less-processed vegan method of cooking, this is one book that can be tried. For me it is somewhat of a disappointment.

Old bones, old murders, new murders--all of them challenge the new deputy of Murfree, Texas (Chris Cherry), who wants to solve local crimes, and isn't content to leave well enough alone. The facts Chris needs to unravel the puzzles he faces are mostly there to find and piece together, but to do that he must defy his boss, Sheriff Stanford "The Judge" Ross. The Judge is a law unto himself in Big Bend County (on the U.S./Mexico border); he's a man respected and feared by all. The Judge (poor man!) has terrible luck with his wives--the first disappeared, the second drowned in the bathtub, and the third (Evelyn) just ran away.

Evelyn's teenage son (Caleb) knows that the Judge must have murdered Evelyn, but has no proof. He and his father share a home, uneasily keeping their distance from each other. Caleb's best friend, a pretty Mexican girl (America), is being stalked by a local sexual predator, and is waiting for her missing brother (border guard Rudy Ray) to return and take her far away from Murfree. A new high school teacher (Anne) has her own secrets to hide, but offers hope for both Caleb and America.

This unusually-plotted novel is Western crime fiction at its best. It presents a remarkable picture of the empty Texas border country. There is a full panoply of well-developed, unforgettable characters, ranging from drug traffickers and addicts to ordinary citizens and crooked lawmen. The story is told in alternating "viewpoint character" chapters (e.g., "1 Chris", "2 Anne", "5 Caleb", "6 Chris"). Generally I hate this technique (because it needs a cliffhanger at the end of each chapter), but author J. Todd Scott displays total mastery, and demonstrates how effective the technique can be for telling a story when it's done right. Only once did I get impatient and read ahead on a single character's chapters to find out more, and later on I kind of regretted having done it.

This is an extremely well-written book. There are plenty of plot twists and turns to keep the reader reading, and the Big Bend County setting is fascinating. I loved it.
