Picking human brains out of her hair is not in the job description, but that is what FBI Profiler Maggie O'Dell is doing when she first appears in this eighth novel in the "Maggie O'Dell" series. Maggie herself is a bit "damaged" by this experience, and by her previous serial killer investigations that involve bloody body parts. But despite her nightmare-induced sleeplessness, and inability to talk things over with her absent friend Colonel Benjamin Platt, Maggie does not hesitate to answer DHS Deputy Director Charlie Wurth's call to investigate a fishing cooler filled with plastic-wrapped body parts that has been recovered from the ocean near Pensacola, Florida by a Coast Guard helicopter rescue team.

Maggie does not hesitate even though Pensacola is directly in the path of an oncoming hurricane, Hurricane Isaac, which is projected to make landfall in a few days as a Category 5 (catastrophic damage) hurricane. Maggie soon meets up with Liz Bailey, the helicopter team's rescue swimmer, who is highly experienced but not yet fully accepted as a member of the team. Liz, who regularly descends on a cable to water level to maneuver injured recreational and commercial sailors into baskets and harnesses for pickup, is every bit as brave and quick-thinking as Maggie when fully engaged in her highly dangerous work.

Early in the book, readers are introduced to the charismatic "Joe Black", who operates a body-parts business that supplies surgeons with bone paste and skin taken from fresh corpses (deceased less than 12 hours), and medical seminars with torsos, hands, and other body parts used for practicing newly-learned surgical techniques. The body-parts business is regulated and legal, but not Joe Black's approach. Joe has figured out that "people disappear after hurricanes", and uses that insight to dramatically increase his business' bottom line. Joe also believes in recycling all possible body parts, even when they aren't too fresh, or are damaged, which forms the basis for a secondary plot that brings Benjamin to Pensacola at the same time as Maggie.

In this well-written page-turner, the "light" suspense is maintained simply by keeping the reader on edge about which persons among the many likeable characters (neither Liz nor Maggie) are going to make Joe Black's acquaintance next. The plot is carefully constructed, and the many diverse threads are pulled together at the end in a satisfying and believable ending. There are developments in Maggie's personal life and character that series fans surely won't want to miss. There is also interesting background on living in "hurricane country", and the "routine" preparations required for riding out a major hurricane.

This novel gets 4.5 stars, rounded up to 5 stars. This is my first Maggie O'Dell novel, and the book works perfectly as a stand-alone, with no apparent spoilers.

I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it.

I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good.

This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top.

In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one.

It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.)

I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker.

I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.

Cooking with smoke is different than just grilling and the results are very different. If you compare a rack of smoked ribs to straight grilled ribs you’ll understand the differences very clearly – there’s more to it than just smoky flavors. This book serves as a good primer how how to cook with smoke. It’s not an absolutely comprehensive tome that covers everything you could ever know, but it’s a great starting point.

The book covers all of the basics – the tools you need, different types of wood and when to use them depending on what you want to cook, techniques, smoke times, and even different cuts of meats. Sriracha has become the latest darling of the culinary world...this addictive blend of chiles, vinegar and garlic is giving traditional hot sauce a run for its money on tables across the country. Hot on the heels of [[ASIN:1607740036 The Sriracha Cookbook: 50 "Rooster Sauce" Recipes that Pack a Punch]], Veggie-Lover's Sriracha Cookbook has 50 vegan "rooster sauce" recipes from drinks and snacks to soups, salads, main dishes, breakfast ideas and desserts. You'll find something to please every palate; there's a healthy dash of the international, from Middle Eastern muhammara and hummus to the Mediterranean, Latin America, Caribbean, and Asia (pho sure!).

One of the greatest features is that yes, this is a vegan cookbook, but each recipe comes with suggestions to adapt recipes for (lacto-ovo) vegetarians as well as gluten-free diets. It's a much-appreciated gesture; I do make vegan dishes from time to time, but I love that the substitutions are right there, so I don't have to mentally convert ground flaxseed and water to egg whites, or ponder how to make gluten-free panko substitutes.

I tried four recipes: the Sriracha caponata (page 27), zippy zucchini zuppa with asparagus and cannellini beans (page 36), the Sriracha broccoli slaw (page 47), and the maple-Sriracha roasted Brussels sprouts with cranberry wild rice (page 87). Next up is the warm Dijon-Sriracha potato salad with toasted hazelnuts, spicy tabbouleh-stuffed dolmas, and the super simple peanut butter and Sriracha cookies w/ chocolate chips!

For my recipe testing, I used two readily-available brands of Sriracha, the ubiquitous [[ASIN:B0002PSOJW Huy Fong, Sriracha Hot Chili Sauce, 17 Ounce Bottle]] and the new Trader Joe's Sriracha sauce. Another awesome option is to use [[ASIN:B0006SKCVI Huy Fong Vietnamese Chili Garlic Sauce, 8 Oz.]] or the straight-up [[ASIN:B000F865ZQ Huy Fong Sambal Oelek Ground Chili Paste - 8 oz x 2 bottles]]- all heat, no garlic or spices. There is also a recipe for making your own Sriracha, but as Randy points out, it is cheaper (and easier) to purchase it! The four recipes I tested were all accurate as written and I found the seasoning levels perfect. If you like a hint of heat without going all the way, start out by using half the amount of Sriracha called for and season to taste.

The cranberry wild rice is going to be my new Thanksgiving standby; it is an addictive blend of toothsome wild rice, cranberries, chopped pecans, and rosemary topped with caramelized Brussels sprouts (the rice minus the Brussels sprouts would make a great filling for halved acorn squash as a vegan holiday entrée). It also makes a stunning centerpiece if you take the time to arrange the Brussels sprouts in rows across the rice (to see my uploaded images including this recipe, click on the "see all editorial reviews" link above). The broccoli slaw was a snap to throw together using bagged broccoli slaw from Trader Joe's; lacking fresh ginger, I threw in some slivered crystallized ginger, and the spicy bite complemented the slaw nicely. The zippy zucchini zuppa was exactly that; I loved the addition of asparagus late in the cooking, as it gave a lovely crunch and color to the soup. The caponata was the first time I'd tried making my own at home, and I loved the combination of sweet (from raisins) and tart (cider vinegar, tomato puree, Kalamata olives).

Along with Randy's signature humor, I love the fact that he uses his own experiences switching to a plant-based diet to sell the merits of these recipes; I find that nothing turns me off quicker than preachy manifestos disguised as cookbooks! You won't find recipes that used processed TVP meat analogs - no chik'n nuggets, vegan corn dogs, or their iffy ilk here, though you will find some tofu-based recipes like Israeli shakshuka, a California Benedict, or quiche Florentine, along with tempeh. If you live in a small town, you may have difficulty finding a few of the ingredients locally, but most ingredients should be easy enough to source or can be ordered online (the most expensive and hard-to-find item here is ackee, or canned jackfruit, used to mimic the texture of pulled pork).

The 50 recipes in "Veggie-Lover's Sriracha Cookbook" offer tasty and quick ways to add more fresh veggies into your diet with a splash of Sriracha. This is comfort food at its best, from Sriracha-cauliflower mac n' cheeze and banh xeo (Vietnamese "crepes" filled with savory fillings) to curried kale and squash risotto, to some snappy tipples like watermelon-Sriracha sangria and mango-Sriracha margaritas that are a perfect way to beat the summer heat. Best of all, Randy's recipes inspired me to start creating my own vegetarian Sriracha-spiked creations; yesterday I made killer ice pops by blending a couple of tablespoons of Sriracha with store-bought watermelon agua fresca, poured into [[ASIN:B000G34F2U Tovolo Star Ice Pop Molds, Set of 6, Green]]and froze, and it was awesome!(spicy popsicles are a Mexican staple; chile mango, chile pineapple or chile tamarind are a common sight from pushcart vendors; more spicy pops can be found in [[ASIN:1607740354 Paletas: Authentic Recipes for Mexican Ice Pops, Shaved Ice & Aguas Frescas]]).

Partial skeins and balls, left over from larger projects, are the bane of every knitter's existence. The yarn is too good to throw out, but there's not enough to actually make anything. However, this book solves the problem, with its many patterns for projects so well designed that, as author Melissa Leapman says, "no one will ever know these projects were made from leftovers!"

The attractive projects include (1) a charted "jigsaw puzzle piece" baby blanket; (2) geometrically-patterned bangle bracelets; (3) striped mittens, scarves, shawls, throws, and sweaters; (4) striped and patterned shopping, sample, and tote bags; (5) a Fair Isle yoked sweater and a Fair Isle vest; and (6) many single-color hats. The projects are grouped in the book according to the yarn weights used: fine, lightweight, worsted, or chunky.

What I really like about this book is the lengthy introduction that discusses sorting yarns leftovers by weight and color, to ensure the best possible combinations for successful knitted fabrics. Several pages, illustrated with color wheels, explain the scientific theory of color--including how to get good results from monochromatic color combinations, and from combinations of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 colors. The book also includes explanations of how to join yarns together using standard knitting techniques, or using the "Russian join" (which uses a tapestry needle). There is a nice discussion of how to put together a "Magic Ball" of short lengths of leftover yarns of different colors and textures (the ball is knitted up like regular yarn); as well as some discussion of yarn storage.

Nearly all of the projects are fairly easy to knit. (The Fair Isle garments, the intarsia sample bag, and the charted puzzle-piece blanket will require moderate knitting experience). Note, though, that whether you will have enough yarn already on hand to knit many of the larger projects will depend entirely on the actual size and makeup of your personal yarn stash! For me, this book rates an unqualified 5 stars.

Tracing vegetarian Jewish Diaspora recipes is no easy task: Rabbi and chef Gil Marks has created a painstakingly researched cookbook that at times reads more like a history book. With recipes from Azerbaijan to Yemen, Olive Trees and Honey is a catalogue of the vast variety of Jewish vegetarian cuisines, including chapters on cheese and dairy spreads, pickles and relishes, soups, salads, savory pastries, cooked vegetable dishes, vegetable stews, beans and legumes, grains, dumplings and pasta, eggs, and sauces and seasonings.

Each section features fascinating information about the origins and spread of each type of cuisine, often with illustrative maps. Some examples include a map of which type of cheeses are popular in which Diaspora community, or the spread of stuffed cabbage from Persia. Each recipe contains a myriad of further variations to try. Every recipe is labeled Dairy or Pareve for those keeping kosher, and many recipes offer Pareve alternatives (which generally are vegan).

Some of the more interesting recipes that caught my eye were Moroccan Pumpkin Soup, Hungarian Wine Soup, a sangria-like cold soup (red wine and fresh/frozen fruit mixed with orange juice, lemon juice, sugar, cinnamon, and cloves), Middle Eastern Bulgur-Stuffed Cabbage, Sephardic Cauliflower Patties (perfect for Passover if made with matza meal), Indian Coconut Rice, Middle Eastern Wheat Berry Stew, and the classic Ashkenazic Sweet Noodle Pudding (Kugel).

Also included are suggested vegetarian menus for special occasions and holidays. This is a monumental work and one of the most beautiful vegetarian cookbooks out there, refreshing for the soul as well as body. I only have two small complaints: Rabbi Gil Marks wrote the excellent (and out-of-print) [[ASIN:0684870037 The World Of Jewish Desserts: More Than 400 Delectable Recipes from Jewish Communities]]. I would have liked to see the incorporation of more of his well-researched desserts as a final sweet note (there are recipes for several pastry-based desserts included). Also, the large number of variations in addition to the core recipes (example: ten recipes for red lentil soup, many of which are minor variations of the basic Sephardic Red Lentil Soup) made this a bit overwhelming; although I enjoyed browsing through the 300+ recipes, I honestly don't see myself ever making more than a handful on a regular basis.

An entertaining, comprehensive biography of Sir Thomas Lipton, who founded the Lipton's retail grocery business in the United Kingdom in the late 19th century, and went on to found the global Lipton's Tea empire that still flourishes today as a Unilever acquisition.

Thomas Lipton's family fled from famine-struck Ireland to Scotland in 1847, only to settle in Glasgow's worst slum, the Gorbals. At age 17, Thomas emigrated to America, where at first he labored in the post-Civil War cotton fields, but later obtained a coveted job at a famous New York City department store, A.T. Stewart's. At A.T. Stewart's, Thomas picked up a bit of retail wisdom that served him well for the rest of his life: "The man who on his trade relies/Must either bust or advertise."

At age 19, Thomas staged a triumphant return (by horse-drawn cab) to his parent's Glasgow home and miniscule grocery shop. Soon after, using his hard-won savings, he opened his first Lipton's grocery. From then on, he applied his advertising genius and amazing entrepreneurial talents to building a chain of successful grocery stores that would always be known for quality goods and low prices.

By age 32, Thomas was a rich man, although he always remained a favorite of commoners on both sides of the Atlantic, even after he became an intimate friend of the Prince of Wales (later King Edward) and regularly associated with millionaires, military heroes, and aristocrats. Throughout his life, Thomas focused on obtaining publicity for Lipton's, making use of "gimmicks"--now seeming rather commonplace--such as delivery trucks emblazoned with "Lipton's", men hired to herd pigs (Lipton's orphans) through Glasgow streets, and giant cheeses (up to 3,500 pounds) that were imported from America, accompanied by parades and transatlantic media coverage. In 1898, Thomas was knighted by Queen Victoria.

From 1899 to 1920, Sir Thomas built four unsuccessful America's Cup challengers (Shamrock I, II, III, IV). About half of A FULL CUP is devoted to these years of Sir Thomas' life. Sir Thomas was always a gracious loser, which he could afford to be, because he was obtaining priceless publicity for the Lipton's empire. A FULL CUP includes quite a bit of historical detail about the preparations for each America's Cup challenge, the races themselves, and the parades and publicity that surrounded each event. However, it is about Sir Thomas Lipton's life, not yacht racing, so it probably adds little to what is already known about the history of the America's Cup races.

A FULL CUP is an example of biography at its best. It presents a well-rounded picture of a truly one-of-a-kind individual, who started with nothing, and, through his own hard work, became one of the wealthiest men in the world, a philanthropist, and a popular hero. In particular, I enjoyed this book because there has always been Lipton's tea on my kitchen pantry shelf. It amazed me to learn that the brand was founded by a single, colorful, successful entrepreneur--a businessman who was far ahead of his time in understanding the value of advertising and publicity.

Hot Bread Kitchen, based in NYC, builds lasting economic security for low-income, immigrant and minority individuals by creating pathways to professional opportunities in the culinary industry. 67% of their operating budget is funded through the sale of multi-ethnic breads and rental of commercial kitchen space. The range of breads that they bake and deliver includes Iran (nan-e-barbari, a chewy flatbread topped with black and white sesame seeds, and nan-e-qandi), Morocco (m'smen, a flaky flatbread traditionally served for breakfast with honey), Mexico (corn tortillas), Eastern Europe (challah), Ethiopia (the slightly sour injera, fermented teff flour served with wat), and more.​

The long-awaited Hot Bread Kitchen Cookbook is divided by bread type: unleavened and flatbreads, lean breads and rolls, enriched breads, rolls, and buns, filled doughs, and quick breads and holiday breads. You'll find favorites from India (paratha, naan, chapatis), the Middle East (hummus, pita), Eastern Europe (challah, matzo, eier kichel, bialys, knishes, kreplach, nut roll), France / Italy (batard, pan bagnat, olive boules, ciabatta) and Mexico / Latin America (pan de muertos, conchas, tortillas, guacamole, tamales, tostadas, empanadas). Other little-known gems include Albanian cheese triangles, Tibetan momos, Another thing I liked was that various recipes are included that use leftover bread, from bread puddings and stale bread (panzanella, tres leches bread pudding with Mexican chocolate sauce, ribollita), to complementary dishes (curry, wat, stews, dips, salads) that pair perfectly with the included bread recipes.

I consider myself a fairly competent home baker; I have long worked with yeast breads (including fresh cake yeast) both kneading by hand and stand mixer, and I welcomed the challenge of new bread types. Step-by-step photos (for trickier items like braiding challah) are particularly helpful for novice bakers. As a longtime baker of challah, I particularly appreciated the many challah recipes, including basic, raisin, whole wheat and Sephardic. You'll even find Vietnamese-style bagueettes and iced Vietnamese coffee.

This lovely selection of breads and accompanying dishes, sauces, and sides is rounded out by baker profiles and a very thorough guide to tips, equipment, and bread storage suggestions. Ingredients are given in US volume and metric (for my baking books, I generally prefer weight measurements, so appreciated having the metric weights given). Gorgeous photos give serving suggestions for each bread and side dish featured in the book. A list of online/mail-order sources and a hefty list of acknowledgments round out the book.

An excellent resource for home bakers, especially if you already have some prior bread baking experience. This is a fantastic treasure trove if you enjoy trying international bread recipes and new dishes; it would be fun to host themed dinners using the included recipes. Highly recommended!

For my entire life I've been interested in keeping myself out of debt mostly due to necessity. I have also done so rather successfully and with amazing results. I made it my mission over the years to learn about the myths and preconceived notions regarding certain debts whether they apply to me or not, such as:

- student loan and child support debt will not be forgiven in bankruptcy
- forgiven debt can be taxed by the IRS as income
- borrowing from a 401K not only results in lost retirement savings but may result in IRS penalties because it is considered a premature withdrawal from your retirement account if the debt is not paid almost immediately upon losing your job
- sometimes it is smarter to rent a place than own your own residence

I've also lived so frugally with only minor exceptions and have employed the following techniques in order to reach a goal, such as:

- turning my A/C or heat off completely; or adjusting the temperatures as suggested in this book
- rarely eating out
- not using an IRS refund as my way of saving
- keeping my car until the "wheels almost fall off"
- shopping at thrift shops

I found the advice in this book to be so sensible and so "reinforcing" to what I do already that I actually got up in the middle of the night to finish reading it. Although most of the stuff I actually knew, I liked that this book reinforced the way I've handled my life so far. There have been people who told me I should buy a house when I was not ready because my rent money was not accruing equity or that I should borrow from my 401K when I was going through a difficult financial time. I did not listen to these people because I knew the pitfalls and this book elaborates on all that.

A seasoned adult will find this book filled with many basic facts that is known to them. However, even a seasoned adult can learn some new facts. For instance, I learned that "consumers can collect up to $1,000 per violation in small claims court" if a debt collector violates the laws governing debt collection. That was news to me.

In my opinion, "Deal with Your Debt" should be required reading for all college-age teenagers before they start acquiring debt and developing dangerous habits. It is filled with common sense strategies and some common and not so common information about debt. It is also a great book for those currently in debt to help reinforce what they know or how they can live more frugally. The text provides a list of choices people can make to reduce their debt as well as stay out of debt in the future. This is a book of options that the reader can make their own based on their circumstances. However, one must be prepared to make difficult decisions because employing these options is not without sacrifice or commitment to the goal of dealing with your debt.

The only improvement I suggest the author make is to include an Appendix that includes the following information from within the book:

1. a table that lists all the websites mentioned and their purpose
2. a reprint of the table that lists the Statutes of Limitations in Years for all states (even though it's searchable in the index)
3. a grouping of all the spending worksheets in one place for those who are interested

In summary, after reading this book I can honestly say I would not have done anything differently but that's because I educated myself about debt for the past 30+ years. "Deal with Your Debt" is really about choices and providing the reader with an understanding of what is and is not fact. As the author states in the beginning of the book, "The hardest part of managing your money can be figuring out the balance between living fully today and preparing for the future." The author stresses that you have to do what is right for your situation and with the facts this book makes it easier to do that.

Cooking with cast iron cookware is a little different than using stainless steel or aluminum pans. Cast iron heats up differently (more evenly) and it retains its heat longer. As such, recipes written with general cookware may work acceptably in cast iron but recipes developed specifically for cast iron tend to work much better. The Lodge Cast Iron Cookbook is filled with fine recipes that work especially well in cast iron cookware, and it also includes a lot of interesting storytelling. That said, there are a few recipes in this collection that are imperfect.

This cookbook is filled with a decent collection of recipes. There are recipes for soups and stews, assorted breakfast items, a very generous chapter on cornbread and even a good choice of dessert recipes. If you have been wondering what you can do with your cast iron and you just don't have an idea of what will work, there's guaranteed to be something in this cookbook that will appeal.

Many of the recipes have full-color pictures, though not all of them do. The photography is beautiful and this cookbook is just as comfortable on the coffee table as it is on the kitchen workbench.

Not all of the recipes are done in the oven. There is one chapter filled with recipes that are designed for use outdoors or on a grill. At one time this is how cooking was done and these recipes will take one back to days past. I have not yet tried making bread in a cast-iron dutch oven on the grill but it's on the short list of "to try" recipes.

Though these recipes are designed for cast iron, some are not perfect. One we tried in particular that proved to problematic was the giant cookie recipe that calls for making the cookie in a 10" skillet and then serving it from there. After baking it for the required time at the correct temperature, it was still very clearly underdone to the point of soupy in large spots. We ended up having to cover the whole top in aluminum foil to slow browning and put it back in the oven for quite a while (close to 20 minutes) before it was done. Note: There's nothing wrong with my oven.

I do think the anecdotes and stories add to this cookbook. Though certainly not required, these additions convey a lot of interesting facts and lore relating to cast iron cooking.

I personally prefer the [[ASIN:1620872609 Cast Iron Cookbook]] by Joanna Pruess.

The Lodge Cast Iron Cookbook is a very nice collection of recipes that comes with beautiful photos and fascinating stories. Some of the recipes fall a little short in the execution, though, and should be adjusted appropriately.

I am a fan of cookbooks and when I was presented an opportunity to buy all 5 of the cookbooks in this series at a very reasonable price I jumped at the chance. So far I have been very pleased.

Favorite Recipes of Home Economics Teachers cookbooks are very similar to cookbooks you would expect to see put out by a church or other fundraising group, though they are larger and are hard-bound. They use the GBC-style binding which is great for laying them flat on the counter when following recipes. The table of contents is somewhat sparse, taking the reader to a general section instead of to specific recipes, but the index at the back is exhaustive and complete.

In addition to the recipes, each of the cookbooks in the series have sections for cooking tips and suggestions, conversion and temperate charts and definitions of common terms before progressing into the recipe collections.

Vegetables has a nice variety of recipes divided into the following sections, which unlike the other cookbooks in the series is arranged semi-alphabetically: Asparagus, Beans, Beets, Broccoli, Cabbage, Carrots, Cauliflower, Corn, Eggplant, Onions, Peas, Potatoes, Spinach, Squash, Sweet Potatoes, Tomatoes, Mixed Vegetables, Foreign Fruits/Vegetables, Fruit Appetizers/Beverages/Salads, Fruit Desserts, Fruit and Vegetable Relishes/Sauces, Fruit and Vegetable Jams/Jellies, and finally Fruit and Vegetable Pickles.

Though including fruit recipes in this collection makes perfect sense and is very welcome, there is no indication from the title that this is a fruit and vegetable collection.

As is typical with the other books in the collection, Vegetables is full of old-fashioned recipe ideas. If you have fond memories of green bean casserole as only your grandmother could make, this just may be the right collection for you. I have marked several recipes to try soon, and every time I pick up this cookbook I find more ideas that I needs to try as well.

It's difficult to find much wrong with any of the cookbooks in the Favorite Recipes of Home Economics Teachers. I have used Vegetables the least but I have been pleased with it nonetheless. It's an excellent collection of recipes that will take you back a few decades and will definitely please the family.

DARK HORSE is the second "Eddy Harkness" novel (the first is THIRD RAIL), but it works fine as a standalone. It's a police procedural, I guess, but it's mainly about Narco-Intel detective Eddy Harkness' adventures, in and around the city of Boston. If you like the rule-bending, cynical, city-hall-fighting detective and his friends, you'll enjoy the book. However, the novel's not a fast-reading, exciting, page-turner--there's too much detail about low-class dives, obscure city charters, data mining, Boston's history, and sleazy crooks for that.

In the novel, Boston's impoverished Lower South End has been evacuated, due to an unexpected hurricane that threatens to flood the area. While clearing out stragglers, Eddy finds a boy (Deaf Kid) chained to a radiator, and rescues him just before a dam breaks and inundates the entire neighborhood. Deaf Kid turns out to be the key to finding out who or what is behind the sudden appearance of Dark Horse, a nearly pure heroin that is doctored to look like cheap black tar heroin and sold on the streets at black tar prices. Dark Horse is causing an epidemic of overdose deaths, and Eddy's Narco-Intel crew wants it off the market.

After the flood, Boston's cleanup efforts for the Lower South End completely stall, so that the low-income residents cannot return to their homes. Mysteriously the residents relocate to nearby Nagog, in accordance with an antique billeting law still on the city's books. What in the world is going on? Could Boston's shiny new mayor and the secretive Boston Harbormasters group be conspiring to take over the Lower South End for their own nefarious purposes?

This novel is extremely well-written. Likable, well-developed characters abound (e.g., Eddy, Patrick, Candace); and there are also quite a few memorable villains (e.g., Mouse, Jennet, Burch, MOM). Because DARK HORSE is interesting and fun, but a bit of a slog, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

EXPENSIVE SENTENCES: DEBUNKING THE COMMON MYTHS THAT DERAIL DECISIONS AND SABOTAGE SUCCESS is a rarity--a business management book with extremely valuable content. Anyone--not just business managers--can profit from reading this book, which explains why "expensive sentences" (generally accepted truisms) should be carefully analyzed to see whether they in fact apply to a real-life situation--because blindly following a truism can cost a lot of money.

There are three types of expensive sentences--sentences about "stuck", "special", and "scarce" situations. Examples are, respectively, "It's too late to turn back now"; "It would be nice if we could do that, but we can't because of ..."; "Nobody else can do what they do".

Author Quarles explains why it can be far more costly to continue on the same path than to "cut bait" and do something else. A persuasive example is Napoleon's decision to continue the French army's march to Moscow during the War of 1812--despite his losing men to disease and freezing temperatures. That decision ultimately brought down Napoleon's entire Empire.

Another easy to understand analysis of an expensive sentence is the one for "the customer is always right". There are many things to consider here, including the fact that customers don't always know what they want--they may say they want a product with a gazillion features, but actually buy and use a simpler product with only a few essential features.

It should be clear that an expensive sentences analysis can apply to a life situation as well as a business situation. There is a lot of food for thought in this excellent book.

I ordered this with my friend's severely autistic son in mind. This very thin book introduces the concept of five love languages that can be used to "love" your spouse and your child or children with disabilities. 

The five languages are:
- Words of Affirmation
- Quality Time
- Gifts (or "Receiving Gifts")
- Acts of Service
- Pysical Touch

Two helpful child development categories ( attachment and cognitive development) are also introduced because it is helpful to know where your child stands with regard to these categories. For children with unhealthy attachments, understanding their type of attachment helps the parent to implement these love languages to provide healing.

These love languages are used between the parents and also between parent and child. For example with regard to physical touch, one father would rub the cheek of his child when in the NICU to provide physical contact and express love. When that disabled child began to talk, his son would beg to have his cheek rubbed as it would soothe him and let him know he felt loved.

In summary, this is an resource for parents with disabled children. The entire premise of this text is to introduce these five love languages and then provide parents with examples of how others implemented them with their children and sometimes with each other. At the beginning there are tests the parent can take to determine their love language. Those tests are also available online.

I believe this book is not only good for those who have disabled children but for any adult in a relationship or with a child. However, I did want more. I would have liked five full case studies on each of these love languages in addition to the many unrelated examples.

THE BONE TREE is a well-written thriller, but it's a sequel to [[ASIN:B00FJ3AC10 Natchez Burning]], which I haven't read. Evidently [[ASIN:B00FJ3AC10 Natchez Burning]] ended with a major cliffhanger, so this book starts out by dealing with the prior book's unresolved issues.

After reading 50 pages, I still wasn't sure who the good guys and bad guys were, or why the good guys and bad guys wanted to kill one another. There's a small-town mayor, journalist, doctor, and local police chief who are apparently on the same side, allied against a corrupt Louisiana state police organization that wants to do . . . what? There is also an FBI investigator who must be a wild card--whether good guy or bad guy, I don't know. At the time the book opens, a number of people have already been kidnapped, assassinated, euthanized, or burned up while opposing one side or the other. Some of the likely good guys are on the run, some aren't.

After scanning the remaining 752 pages, I threw in the towel. The book seems to be a chronicle of various pursuits and narrow escapes and successful murders, with one side or the other temporarily gaining the upper hand. Also, there's a lot about the involvement of the corrupt state police organization in the assassinations of JFK and RFK. This is a plot that I cannot get interested in--and I simply lack the time to slog through such a long book when there's no entertainment value in it for me.

No doubt those who read and enjoyed the very-well-reviewed [[ASIN:B00FJ3AC10 Natchez Burning]] will be eager to read THE BONE TREE to learn what happened next. As for me, I have no plans to read [[ASIN:B00FJ3AC10 Natchez Burning]], even though I have already purchased a copy on the basis of its excellent reviews. I already know that I don't care for the characters, or for the plot that centers on police corruption at the highest levels. As a matter of personal preference in mystery/thriller novels, I rate THE BONE TREE at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

I decided to buy a pair of noise canceling headphones after moving to a different location at work where I am in closer proximity to a rack of computers that runs constantly. After a short while the whirr of the fans in the computers and the rack in which they are mounted gets very tiring and annoys the ears. After doing some research, I finally decided on the Bose QuietComfort 15, and almost immediately I have seen that I made the right choice.

I was fortunate enough to get my hands on one of these before I committed my money so I could test the quality. I was very pleased when I put on the headphones, turned them on and all of the ambient noise around me simply vanished. The sound of the air conditioning, the murmuring of people chatting around me, even traffic outside was reduced to such a degree that I felt like I was in a bubble. I bought them on the spot.

I put these headphones through two major tests outside of work.

First, I plugged them into my iPod and turned them on. All I could hear when the music played was the music. Talking around me was overcome by the noise cancellation and the music, which was not set to a particularly high volume. As many have commented, the bass is very rich with these headphones but that's fine with me, as I really appreciate good bass response. Treble and mid-range are also good, though not quite as bright as the bass.

The really big surprise was when I plugged them into the mixing board where I was doing live recording. I was shocked at how effectively I could hear every sound coming through the microphones but practically nothing else. The sound was clear, crisp and not muddied in any way I could ascertain, which gave me a much better idea of what was recording onto the CD. I had used a lesser headset for this purpose, but no longer.

Some noises do get through, such as loud talking and even the typing on my keyboard, but those sounds are muffled quite a bit. The idea is to eliminate droning, obnoxious noise such as engine noise (there are several mentions in the documentation about wearing these on planes), while still allowing certain things to get through. These are certainly not perfect in that regard but they do come close.

In the past I have bought headphones only from either Sony or Sennheiser, with a very strong bias for the latter. This is my first set of Bose headphones and they are definitely the best pair I have ever used (let alone owned). I regard these as very much worth the price and gladly recommend them for anyone wanting to hear nothing but the music without blasting out the ears. These are high quality earphones and will please the enthusiast looking for good sound as well as the traveler looking for a quiet ride.

John's revelation has been an issue for many since its inception. In terms of interpretation, many have painted and illustrated what they envision when reading this confounding book (the back of this graphic novel even explains so). This adaptation is one of the best I've ever seen, both in terms of imagination and expression. It's true that cinema has changed art forever, and we are now better able to mimic emotion in art. The fact that John is shown every now and then, showing reaction to what he is witnessing, adds a whole other layer of adapting his revelation into the art form, let alone graphic medium.

Koelle, the artist, and Dorff, the art director, have done a magnificent job at showing their imaginative sides in this story, and the end result is nothing short of masterful. I've read the actual account from the NIV and NLT, coming out confused and wondering. I like to humbly boast that I have a capable imagination, but even I had a hard time deciphering and/or picturing John's visions. It may be human error (it most likely is), but when I came upon the illustration for the locusts, I realized this graphic novel nailed it. The pacing and text edits are fantastic, to the point, and well placed. The artwork itself easily rivals some of the best I've seen in current big-name titles (namely Marvel and The New 52 DC, not to mention others), but the fact that they took it one step further and tried to add some sort of cohesion to the bizarre beasts and actions (e.g., the locusts I mentioned above, as well as the angelic beings) solidifies this graphic novel as one of the best I've read.
Heck, I think that, from now on, I'll take these illustrations as my source of reference!

This book is well worth your time and investment. It's not as lengthy as the actual text itself, considering they use the text in a way that fits panel to panel, but the editing by Frs. Arey and Sevastiades is remarkable. Koelle and Dorff don't add the icing to the cake; they add to the cake itself.
My only complaint is that I feel the panel to panel layout restricts some art direction. I feel they could've played around with some layouting, maybe eliminate some panels and use other borders (such as globes), thus freeing from the standard square-to-rectangle-to-square-to-full page scheme. Still, it doesn't detract from the overall experience.

As for export/import, I obviously need more knowledge about different formats and 3D packages. This book does go into Modo files with Maya, but since I don't have access to Maya I was limited on what I could learn there.

3D printing has really taken off in the last few years and I have seen printed objects made as toys as well as prototypes prior to production. Objects generated on a 3D printer start with ideas and designs get built around those ideas before they can be actually printed. This book is designed to be an idea book for those who want to create things with their printers, and it is a commendable effort. I do have a couple of complaints, though.

First off, this is not a comprehensive book on all the possibilities of what you can do with your printer. It’s an idea book that’s aimed more at beginners, and it has a lot of different how-to projects that serve as good starting points for more complex projects. It does have a few complete projects too such as a cookie cutter. In each case, the book gives step by step instructions on what to do, though there’s some places where generalities are required due to system variations.

It’s in these variations that this book has one of its stumbling blocks. Because of the wide possibilities in configuration, it is very unlikely that readers will have the exact configuration so there’s some interpretive reading required, particularly when it comes to software. This is ok, but it is presumptuous to assume that everyone will go out and get the same software.

My other complaint is with the physical medium itself. The book’s pages feel like comic book paper. My experience with this kind of paper is that it tends to tear easily. I am not sure how long this book will hold up under heavy use, but I suspect it will be less durable than if it had been printed on better paper.

This book is a commendable effort and it helps the beginner figure out where to start. The price is reasonable and the projects are relatively easy and straightforward. That said, there’s some room for improvement.

OK, I'll admit it, the only reason I got this book was to impress a girl with a perfect meal and I was very taken in by the title and description. I was hoping that this book would unlock the mysteries to making the perfect meal. And to a degree it does. It takes a lot of disparate research and pulls it together so show how different senses, beyond taste, that affect the meal.

The book reads like Freakonomics for the kitchen. The research that it pulls is varied and often very surprising. It is somewhat loosely organized around chapters on expected things like plating, atmosphere and the science of taste, and some surprising ones like eating in the dark. Some of the research seems to be tossed into these categories, but the research is interesting.

The reason I didn't give the book 5 stars is because it was a little academic and it didn't really hit the bullseye with me. The chapter on naming and describing food was nice, but for my date night purposes it was not needed. As were all the restaurant and menu specific stuff. But on the other hand much of this book was fascinating and I truly appreciated the chapters on plating, cutlery and atmosphere. I have to admit, I did skip some areas that were very restaurant specific, but got a lot of value out of the book. At the very least it was an entertaining read. But I have a list of things to try on the next dinner date. Wish me luck.

Sleep Tight introduces Rose Gifford, a DC who still has a learning curve.  The only mother she ever knew was Adele, her grandmother. I would have liked Rose to be written with more depth and complexity, but this is the first entry in a series and I anticipate the character will be developed further.  The plot of this story is quite original.  Women who experience parasomnia, a sleep disorder that can include hallucinations and a sense of paralysis are experiencing a sense that a man who they dream of and who causes night terrors is in fact real.  As Rose and her senior partner Mack investigate, she inexplicably draws the attention of DI Money from a unit everyone things has to do with compliance. But does it?  This is a highly original police procedural, using a terrible sleep disorder as a jumping off point for some paranormal happenings.  Rose, desperate not to be different, is drawn into a new understanding of her gifts as the navigates her work in the  MET, where she gets into trouble as a newbie, partly because she inadvertently learned something about her boss, while being drawn to Mooney's unit.  I thoroughly enjoyed the solution and the paranormal aspects.

I consider myself to be a skilled amateur when it comes to photography – I have a good eye for what makes a good photograph and I have some natural ability but I am not skilled enough or trained enough to be professional. All of what I know about photography has been self-taught and I am always looking for resources from which I can learn new things or get ideas. I looked to this book hoping to get some words of wisdom. While it is a good resource and there’s a lot of useful information within, I don’t necessarily agree with everything this book offers.

The idea behind this book is solid. Multiple professional photographers offer up their thoughts on essential skills that separate a good photographer from a world-class photographer. This covers a broad swath of ideas from workflow to post-processing advice to equipment choices. This is all good stuff and each of these photographers has chosen these bits of advice based on their own experiences.

However, I don’t necessarily agree with some of the advice and it even clashes with that of other professionals. A prime example of that is “don’t ever crop your photos”. The photographer stating this makes a good point – setting up your shot such that you don’t have to crop is good practice and will train you to visualize better, but in the field it isn’t always practical or even possible.

Fortunately, these types of entries are not widespread.

The book breaks up the material into three main sections: “Making Photographs”, “Being a Photographer”, and “Professional Practice”.

The first section, “Taking Photographs”, offers suggestions on the process of actually taking pictures. These are not the rules that rank beginners learn such as how aperture, ISO and shutter speed work together, but instead covers a broad range of more abstract stuff as well as some semi-basic stuff. Examples include “shoot manual”, “use prime lenses” and “see like a child”. The second section, “Being a Photographer”, is more abstract than the first and covers more intellectual and ethical ideas. These include “shoot what you love”, “think like an amateur” (related to the first), and “look inside yourself”. The third section, “Professional Practice”, is even more abstract and though is aimed more at professional photographers it is suitable for the serious amateur as well. Examples include “know why you are doing the work”, “support others” and “don’t assume”.

An absolute beginner at photography will probably be a little overwhelmed by this book but will still find some good nuggets of wisdom and advice. A more skilled amateur like me will find much more use in such, and of course the professional looking to up their game will find more still. That said, it’s important to keep in mind that every photographer is different and there are some ideas herein that won’t necessarily agree with everyone.

ONLY TO SLEEP: A PHILIP MARLOWE NOVEL meshes beautifully with what I remember of Raymond Chandler’s novels. It features hard-boiled private investigator Philip Marlowe, working his last case, and is a convincing portrayal of the classic character. Central to the novel is its evocation of the atmosphere of Southern California and Mexico. The novel makes me want to reread Chandler’s mysteries, which I think is the ultimate proof that author Osborne has succeeded in writing this new Philip Marlowe book at the request of Raymond Chandler’s estate.

In the novel, a pair of insurance fraud investigators visit Marlowe in Baja California; they hire him to investigate the odd circumstances surrounding an insured real estate developer’s drowning death. The developer’s widow (Dolores) ordered the body immediately cremated in Mexico, rather than shipped home to the United States, which raises a big red flag.

Marlowe, like the investigators, suspects that the developer (Donald Zinn) is still alive. Zinn was living far above his means, and facing certain bankruptcy. Marlowe’s inquiries take him first to San Diego, and later to various locations in Mexico, where he determines that his suspicions are correct--but now he must deal with the Zinns’ fraudulent payout, which is filthy, bad-luck money.

The plot has interesting twists and turns, and the 72-year-old Marlowe’s ruminations on old age are well done. The prose style is totally consistent with Chandler’s style in the Philip Marlowe novels. In sum, this is a highly entertaining mystery with some literary qualities.

NO MAN'S LAND is the fourth "John Puller" book, and my first, but it works fine as a standalone. (The first book in the series is ZERO DAY). The main character, Army detective Puller, is a real bulldog of an investigator and a terrific fighter, but he's kind of straight-laced and sort of drab. In contrast, one of the novel's villains--a surgically enhanced soldier programmed to kill any person standing in front of him--is among the more fascinating villains you'll ever run across in a mystery/thriller.

In the novel, Puller is attending his father, a retired 3-star general who has reached the final stages of Alzheimer's, when military investigators arrive at Puller's door with bad news. A dying woman has written a letter accusing the general of having murdered his wife Jackie. Jackie mysteriously vanished from the Fort Monroe army base some 30 years before, when Puller was a small child. Because the general cannot defend himself, Puller takes on the case--and encounters so much stonewalling from his higher ups that it's clear that whatever happened to Jackie is part of a massive Army/government cover-up. When Puller refuses to drop his investigation, he puts his life, and the life of his friend Veronica Knox, in great peril.

A secondary plot (which unfolds in chapters alternating with the chapters about Puller's investigation) describes the activities of the super-soldier killer (Paul Rogers). Rogers has just been released from prison, and is determined to find and kill the man (Chris Ballard) and the woman (Claire Jericho) who many years ago gave him superhuman strength, but took away his ability to feel, and his humanity.

Eventually Puller's and Rogers' paths cross, and eventually all of the complicated threads of the two stories are tied up in an unguessable, but highly satisfying ending. The novel is well-written, but rather slow-moving. The main setting of Fort Monroe, Virginia, is beautifully described. Because I found Puller boring, but Rogers fascinating, I rate NO MAN'S LAND at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

Ghillie Basan, author of several cookbooks on Turkish and Middle Eastern cuisine including [[ASIN:1848859848 Classic Turkish Cooking]] and [[ASIN:1845979486 Tagines & Couscous: Delicious Recipes for Moroccan One-pot Cooking]], offers up a vegetarian (mostly vegan) Moroccan feast in "Vegetarian Tagines & Couscous." Although at first glance this would appear to be a slim volume (65 recipes total), "Vegetarian Tagines & Couscous" is a wonderful all-in-one source for Moroccan pantry staples, light mezze and appetizers, creative ways to make the most of seasonal vegetables and produce, and wonderful couscous and fruit salads that are welcome any time of year. The ingredients and instructions are clearly laid out, and most ingredients should be readily available at your local supermarket. Most of the recipes can be easily made vegan by swapping out agave for honey, using olive oil in place of butter, or by omitting the cheese and eggs (there are relatively few recipes that call for either).

Beginning with essential recipes such as preserved lemons, smen, harissa, chermoula, and ras el hanout, the book offers a diverse selection of light appetizers including cracked green olives and cardamom and harissa, crudités with red chilli dukkah dip, filo fingers stuffed with feta, olives, and preserved lemon, smoked aubergine and yogurt dip with harissa, and strained yogurt and cucumber dip with rose petals. There are also several flavor-infused soups like creamy pumpkin soup with ginger and chilli honey and chilled almond and garlic soup.

The included tagines (both light and hearty) offer a wide range of preparations of vegetables and legumes including the wonderful tagine of artichokes, broad beans, apricots and almonds, onion, olive, and egg tagine with zahtar, and tagine of spicy roasted pumpkin wedges with lime. There are also a number of fruit tagines including the tagine of roasted pear with figs, walnuts and cardamom, stuffed prune tagine with walnuts and rosewater, and pumpkin, apple, and sultana tagine with chermoula, that are a wonderful way to braise fruit to a soft, creamy consistency. I enjoyed the stuffed prune tagine with its spiced wine reduction over Greek yogurt in the mornings!

The cooking instructions for the several couscous dishes yield a light, fluffy couscous unlike the "typical" American boxed couscous. True Moroccan couscous is made fresh and is slowly steamed and fluffed until light and airy. The couscous recipes here are a compromise between the two methods, yielding light, fluffy couscous without the long time steaming, fluffing, adding liquid and repeating. Ghillie has you first soak the couscous in warm water, then fluff the grains with a fork to separate, rub oil into the grains using your fingers, then aerate before baking to heat through. I attempted the couscous with dried fruit and nuts and it turned out every bit as beautiful (and delicious) as the cover photo! You'll also find the traditional couscous with seven vegetables as well as a saffron couscous with roasted coconut and pistachios, couscous with hot apricot chutney and halloumi (the recipe for the homemade chutney is worth the cost of the book alone!), and harissa couscous with pine nuts and fried eggs.

One important word of caution is that your type of tagine and stovetop may result in many of these being prepared in a dish other than a tagine as many of the tagines are cooked on the stovetop versus oven; I have a ceramic stovetop and two clay tagines and was advised not to use clay/terra cotta tagines even with a heat diffuser, so for the many stovetop preparations I used my 4.5-quart Staub Dutch oven instead. If you have a Staub or Le Creuset cast iron tagine, then you should be fine using them directly on a ceramic stovetop.

One of my favorite parts (and a wonderful way to close out a meal) is the gorgeous fruit salads; I made the orange and date salad with chillies and preserved lemon and grapefruit and pomegranate salad with rosewater (see photo); these quickly became favorites and I make them at least every other week now. They are easy to put together and the flavors work wonderfully together, not to mention the striking presentation (I like to fan out the orange segments into a star shape). The contrast between sweet and tart (the preserved lemons), or fruity and floral, serves to balance out spicier dishes or as an anytime treat. Several basic jams and pickle recipes are also included (tomato jam with cinnamon and roasted sesame seeds, lemon, coriander and mint jam, pickled pears with saffron and cinnamon, date relish, and pickled red chillies and purple turnips).

The book's graphic layout and photography by Steve Painter is also stunning, featuring vibrant piles of spices, silks, and gorgeous tilework interspersed throughout. There are full-page, full-color photos for nearly every finished dish.

I find myself turning to "Vegetarian Tagines & Couscous" frequently for the many creative, delicious takes on traditional Moroccan stews; there is plenty of variety to keep you experimenting happily for many weeks or months to come!

Failed Tibetan lama Tenzing "Ten" Norbut is a great private investigator, but his mystery series is NOT for everyone. The novels are slow-paced, as Norbut constantly contemplates his inner equilibrium; and the novels always include some explanation of the teachings of Buddhism (smoothly incorporated into the story, but they're there). A fun element of each novel is Ten's adoption (at the beginning) of a new Rule to live by--a Rule which he usually breaks almost immediately. As Ten himself says in THE FIFTH RULE OF TEN: "That was the problem with setting a new intention: it was invariably, immediately put to the test."

The Tenzing Norbut novels work fine as standalones (the first one, of course, is THE FIRST RULE OF TEN). This fifth novel is my least favorite, because it delves into the difficult-to-understand (for the Western mind) mysticism of the Kalachakra tradition in Tibetan Buddhism. However, the reader doesn't need to understand the tradition to follow the complex plot, and the novel is a must-read for Ten fans because it contains so much of Ten's personal backstory.

In the novel, Ten adopts a new intention to "be mindful both making and keeping commitments that they be springboards to liberation, instead of suffering, for all sentient beings." Ten is tested by a promise made to his autistic housekeeper Kim, and by his promise to marry girlfriend Julie (when he's feeling suffocated by their constant togetherness in their small living quarters). There's hope for Ten, though, because his close friends, lamas Yeshe and Lobsang, have arrived in Los Angeles from Tibet for a fund-raising tour sponsored by Ten's local temple.

Unfortunately, Ten's attention is distracted from the tour. He's pulled into the investigation of a missing person, after receiving a driver's license hand-delivered to his mailbox; and L.A. detective friend Bill is consulting him about a "murder victim outline" found in a local park--worthy of attention, even without a dead body, because it's painted in blood. Also, Ten is having nightmares that finally drive him to seeking psychiatric treatment from his mentor Eric.

Happily, Ten's cat Tank is still around, now coexisting peacefully with Julie's dog Homer. As usual, the characters are well-developed and the plot has many complex twists and turns. However, because the Kalachakra theme slows the story down (more than the Buddhist aspects usually do), I rate THE FIFTH RULE OF TEN at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

MURDER IN PLAIN ENGLISH: FROM MANIFESTOS TO MEMES is a serious academic work, co-authored by a literary criminology professor and an anthropology professor. The book is an examination of "murder" and murderers, using a "literary criminology" approach. This approach is defined as "the study of crime through the lens of literature and language"; it is an approach that includes "the study of half-baked literary attempts by the murderers themselves."

The word "half-baked" clues the reader that this is an opinionated study. Personally, I don't find the authors' analyses of the murderers' writings at all persuasive. For example, in analyzing O.J. Simpson's "suicide letter" (from the time of the infamous "slow speed chase"), they see O.J.'s statement, "First, everyone understand that I have nothing to do with Nicole's murder", as "a weak denial or avoidance strategy" that fails to "assert that he did not kill Nicole". To me, it seems to assert flatly that he did not kill Nicole--but the authors obviously read more into the words and context than I would.

Another example of the authors' opinionated approach is their stated view that "Jack the Ripper" never existed--that he was a figure created by unscrupulous, slanted newspaper coverage that was designed purely to increase newspaper sales. They explain their reasons for adopting this view, and they could be right--I'm not enough of Ripper scholar to be able to evaluate it.

This book amounts to an impressive catalog of murderers--the famous and the not so famous (not just Zodiac and Bundy, but also Hennard and Birnie). The murderers are classified by general types (e.g., the family annihilator, the set-and-run killer), and also by psychopathic types (e.g., the spineless psychopath, the unprincipled psychopath).

The book is probably assigned as a text in some of the authors' college courses. I'm glad that I'm not required to study it closely, because it seems to me that the authors are imposing their preconceived ideas on the facts, instead of reasoning from facts to conclusions. Despite all the facts and analysis included in this book, at the end I didn't feel that I had any greater understanding of murder and murderers than when I started.

I have settled on the English Standard Version (ESV) as my main translation of choice and I have used it for reading and study for years. Like any translation it is not perfect but it is a solid and reliable work that presents the Scriptures is very readable and understandable wording without losing the original context. For cases where historical or theological context is needed for proper understanding, a study Bible comes in very handy. This particular volume is a nice, compact one, though it does have its drawbacks, mainly in the font size.

The main differences between a typical study Bible and this one are more or less obvious - they print is a lot smaller, the margins are more narrow, and the paper is razor thin. The small size is convenient for travel, and it packs wonderfully in a desk drawer or on a shelf in an office. It’s very affordable too, much more so than a full-sized study Bible. The nicest feature of this particular study Bible is actually the nice leatherette cover which protects it from scuffs and scratches, making it an ideal companion when on the road. For people with less than good eyesight though, this Bible will be a struggle to read because of the small typeface.

The study notes are excellent and add a lot in the way of historical context as well as word meanings. This is what a study Bible should be, and it succeeds in that regard.

This is a small and compact study Bible that’s perfect for the traveler or for giving as a gift. I would hesitate to use it as my main study Bible just based on the font size alone, but it’s a good budget option for those that want a study Bible that doesn’t break the bank and doesn’t weigh a ton or take up large amount of room.

The directed focus of this book aims to bestow upon readers a feeling of competent proficiency, and the basic knowledge to safely execute the mindful administration of prescribed, lifesaving treatments through a holistic approach. It is a reference manual that serves as a handy guidebook for caretakers and providers and is presented in an easily approachable format that serves as an added asset to previously established healthcare training techniques.

Perfect for the continuing education of any student, provider, or client seeking further comprehension of and exposure to the common medical practices of adequate documentation and administration of medications through the majority of available routes of drug delivery.

The case study, interactive pre/post-tests, and abbreviation table were incredibly helpful components for enhancing a successful grasp of the material. Diabetes management can be a complex topic to thoroughly outline and explain, but I think this workbook succeeds in making the information accessible to the common layperson.

The authors of this book have identified common problems associated with the use and dispensation of medications and have thereby set forth guidelines for adopting safe practices beneficial to both caregivers and clients. If followed properly, this guidebook is intended to serve as a learning resource that has been designed to “help reduce medication errors, enhance knowledge and improve medication safety.”

Written with the goal of assisting PSWs, UCPs and family caregivers in proficiently managing the task of medication administration, this text has been based upon the theory of phenomenology, which refers to the meaning of the lived experience. A concept founded by two German philosophers, it suggests that each client be treated with unique individuality, to the maximum degree possible within the much-regulated, task-oriented setting of medication administration guidelines.

This reference manual is divided into 3 modules: Enhancing Medication Safety, Medication Administration Techniques, and Insulin Administration and Diabetes Management (as they apply to a community setting). The incredibly detailed and thorough table of contents offers a handy quick search feature for the rapid finding of applicable page numbers at a glance. For litigious reasons, a waiver and release form appropriately appears prior to Module 1, strongly suggesting the participant’s dated signature in order to proceed.

The modules feature learning objectives, key terms, and a short pretest consisting of true/false, multiple choice, and (check all that apply) queries. There is a medical abbreviation worksheet that allows readers to fill in the blanks, and there are numerous examples of sample grid tables showing doctor’s orders and procedural checklists, where the necessary components of each are outlined. A thought-provoking case study appears in the 2nd module where the reader is instructed to reflect upon the factors that contributed to the medication error presented, and a sample prescription drug label allows the reader to practice familiarizing themselves with pharmaceutical details commonly encountered.

Each module concludes with a summary paragraph and a post-test. I am a strong proponent of healthcare texts that encouragingly promote active participation from the reader, and the handy answer keys for all exercises appear at the back of the book.

Topics of polypharmacy, therapeutic windows, potential compliance, oxygen therapy, needle systems, the illness response, impact on ADLs, routes of delivery and medication reconciliation are all addressed. Example tables of medication administration records (MARs) are also shown for clarity and completeness.

I believe this book would be an appropriate and beneficial reference guide and workbook for any caregiver (friend, relative, neighbor) in a home health setting or for any individual tasked with self-administration of their own prescriptions or injection meds. It would also serve as an easily comprehensible and appropriate textbook for students interested in a future in healthcare.

Since this is a Canadian publication, the specific regulations, initiatives, policies, procedures and practice guidelines mentioned within are somewhat country of origin specific and may not fully translate and agree with the same dispensation guidelines and pharmacy practices observed throughout the U.S. and other countries.

I love that the reviewer quote chosen to appear on the book’s cover summarily states: “The knowledge I gained can be applied to the elderly and to anyone that I am administering medications to…” but it’s even more impactful that it ends with the disclaimer “within my limits.” As an osteopathic physician myself, I feel that was an important and realistic distinction for the authors to highlight.

While the content itself has been thoughtfully compiled and arranged, the printed and grammatical presentation of the current edition has some typographical and grammatical mistakes that need further revision.

For more information about receiving a certificate of completion or participating in a Medication Administration workshop sponsored by the Peak Excellence Centre, contact information is conveniently provided for readers on the book’s back cover.
